597:  `k`-tuples per pair of modes and two endpoint formulas, with
598:  `Relation.ReflTransGen` supplying the closure. Modes are what tuples of
599:  elements cannot supply – a one-element universe has one tuple – and play the
600:  role tags play in an interpretation. It is the logic in which REACH is stated
601:  head-on (`DescriptiveComplexity.reach_tcDefinable`) and in which
602:  Immerman–Szelepcsényi is proved, the bridge that gives `REACH ∈ NL`, the
603:  clausal fragments defining only the complement.
604:* `DescriptiveComplexity.TwoCnf` – the criterion for 2-satisfiability ([Aspvall,
605:  Plass & Tarjan 1979][aspvall1979linear]) with no logic in it at all: over a
606:  finite type of variables, a 2-CNF is satisfiable iff no literal reaches its
607:  own negation and back in the implication graph. It is needed once for CNF
608:  structures (2SAT ∈ PTIME) and once for the atoms of a Krom program (turning a
609:  Krom definition into a transitive closure); the two differ only in what plays
610:  the part of a variable.
611:* `DescriptiveComplexity.KromImplication` and
612:  `DescriptiveComplexity.KromTransitiveClosure` – **the converse translation**: the
613:  complement of an SO-Krom definable problem is FO(TC) definable
614:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.TCDefinable.compl_of_sigmaSOKromDefinable`). A Krom program
615:  instantiated in a structure *is* a 2-CNF, whose variables are the atoms of
616:  its block at tuples of elements, so it is satisfiable exactly when no goal
617:  clause fires and no literal reaches its own negation and back
618:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.KromImpl.exists_holds_iff`); the second file expresses the
619:  implication graph as first-order transition formulas
620:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.KromTC.realize_edgeF`) and walks the cycle-witnessing graph
621:  of `DescriptiveComplexity.TwoCnf.carryReach_iff`, the start literal, the current one
622:  and the flag being the mode and the two atoms' arguments the two halves of
623:  the tuple. With the direction below it gives `co-NL(Krom) = NL(TC)`
624:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NL_iff_tcDefinable_compl`); `NL(Krom) = NL(TC)`, and
625:  with it `REACH ∈ NL`, needs the complementation of FO(TC) itself, which is
626:  `DescriptiveComplexity.TCDefinable.compl`.
627:* `DescriptiveComplexity.TransitiveClosureKrom` – the translation that *is* free:
628:  the complement of an FO(TC) definable problem is SO-Krom definable
629:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.SigmaSOKromDefinable.compl_of_tcDefinable`), hence in NL, by
630:  the program guessing the nodes from which an accepting node is reachable, one
631:  `k`-ary relation variable per mode. `DescriptiveComplexity.unreach_mem_NL` is its
632:  single-mode, arity-one instance, written out by hand as a worked example.
633:* `DescriptiveComplexity.InductiveCounting` and `DescriptiveComplexity.TransitiveClosureCompl` –
634:  **FO(TC) is closed under complement** (`DescriptiveComplexity.TCDefinable.compl`), by
635:  inductive counting. The machine is combinatorial, on an abstract finite
636:  linearly ordered node set: eight registers, each a node or a count read as a
637:  rank, and four nested loops – the stages, the outer scan, the inner scan and
638:  a certifying walk – that compute `|Rset (d+1)|` from `|Rset d|`, the count
639:  check leaving a guessed set of layer nodes no room to be too small. The
640:  first-order layer stores a register as one `k`-tuple beside a mode kept in
641:  the control, so a configuration *is* a mode with an `8k`-tuple, and compiles
642:  every atomic constraint of the machine into a formula once the modes are
643:  known – mode-level conditions (“the least mode”, “this mode covers that
644:  one”) being decided outside the formula.
645:* `DescriptiveComplexity.ImmermanSzelepcsenyi` – **`NL = coNL`**
646:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.NL_eq_coNL`), assembled from the complementation of FO(TC)
647:  and the two translations against the Krom fragment. It also gives what those
648:  translations alone could not: NL *is* FO(TC)
649:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.tcDefinable_iff_mem_NL`), the Krom fragment is closed under
650:  complement, and `REACH ∈ NL` (`DescriptiveComplexity.reach_mem_NL`).
651:* `DescriptiveComplexity.TransitiveClosureReach` – **REACH is NL-complete**
652:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.REACH_NL_complete`), the discharge of FO(TC) into its
653:  canonical problem. Unlike the clausal discharges, this one emits nothing: the
654:  graph of the walk of a `DescriptiveComplexity.TCSpec` already *is* a marked graph –
655:  a node is a mode with a `k`-tuple, which is exactly the universe
656:  `Tag × A^dim` of a tagged interpretation – so the three defining formulas are
657:  the specification's own, relabelled
658:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.reach_hard_of_tcDefinable`). No junk arises, so the
659:  reduction needs no relativization; the one adjustment is
660:  `DescriptiveComplexity.TCSpec.pad`, adding a spare mode so that the tag type is
661:  nonempty, since a reduction must map nonempty structures to nonempty ones.
662:  UNREACH is complete too (`DescriptiveComplexity.UNREACH_NL_complete`), by
663:  complementing that reduction – which is again `NL = coNL`, each fragment
664:  defining only one of the two problems head-on.
665:* `DescriptiveComplexity.TransitiveClosureDet` and
666:  `DescriptiveComplexity.TransitiveClosurePull` – FO(DTC), and closure of both
667:  reachability logics under reductions. Determinism is a *formula*, not a side
668:  condition: a `DescriptiveComplexity.TCSpec` is read through
669:  `DescriptiveComplexity.TCSpec.det`, which conjoins to each transition the statement
670:  that no other transition leaves the current node – a finite conjunction over
671:  the modes, the mode comparison being static. Every specification then denotes
672:  a deterministic walk and nothing has to be preserved by a pullback, which is
673:  what makes the closure argument syntactic. The pullback itself
674:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.TCSpec.comap`) walks the interpreted structure while
675:  writing everything on the base one: `k` tags ride along in the mode, the
676:  coordinates flatten to a `k · d`-tuple, and the resulting bijection of nodes
677:  carries steps to steps – whence determinism travels for free, “no competing
678:  successor” being invariant under a bijection.
679:* `DescriptiveComplexity.DetLogSpace` – the class `DescriptiveComplexity.LOGSPACE`
680:  (named in full, `L` being a vocabulary everywhere in this development),
681:  defined by FO(DTC) definability. It is the first class here defined by an
682:  operator-as-data logic rather than by the shape of a kernel: no fragment of
683:  ∃SO comparable to SO-Horn or SO-Krom is known for deterministic logarithmic
684:  space. `DescriptiveComplexity.LOGSPACE_subset_NL` is a determinized walk being a
685:  walk, followed by the FO(TC)/SO-Krom translation.
686:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Game` – **GAME, alternating reachability**
687:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.GAME`), and `DescriptiveComplexity.game_mem_PTIME`.
688:  An AND/OR graph is a directed graph whose nodes are split between two players,
689:  with a set of nodes that win outright; a node is winning when it wins
690:  outright, or belongs to the existential player and *some* successor wins, or
691:  belongs to the universal player, *has* a successor and *all* its successors
692:  win. Read with the universal player removed those are the three clauses of
693:  `DescriptiveComplexity.REACH`, so this is reachability with alternation – one
694:  operator more, one class up. A universal node with no successor **loses**,
695:  which is the convention `DescriptiveComplexity.ATMData.AltWin` already uses,
696:  and matching them is what will let an alternating machine's configuration
697:  graph be an instance with nothing to adjust. Membership is FO(LFP)
698:  definability (`DescriptiveComplexity.game_lfpDefinable`) with one twist: the
699:  universal clause is not a Horn body, so a second relation variable computes
700:  “every successor at least `y` wins” by a scan of the order from its greatest
701:  element down (`DescriptiveComplexity.order_induction_down`). Hardness
702:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.game_PTIME_hard`) is unit propagation read as a game:
703:  variables are existential nodes, clauses universal ones, a clause with no
704:  negative literal wins outright, and the goal clauses are the marked starts, so
705:  the existential player wins exactly when the Horn formula is
706:  *un*satisfiable – hardness of the complement, carried back by
707:  `DescriptiveComplexity.piP_zero_eq`, the same last step CVP's hardness takes.
708:  Whence `DescriptiveComplexity.game_PTIME_complete`.
709:* `DescriptiveComplexity.MachinesAltSpace` and
710:  `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.MachineAltSpace` – **alternating acceptance in
711:  bounded space** (`DescriptiveComplexity.ATMAcceptSpace`), the EXPTIME
712:  candidate. It is `DescriptiveComplexity.ATMData.AltAccepts` with the step
713:  budget dropped, exactly as `DescriptiveComplexity.TMData.AcceptsSpace` is
714:  `DescriptiveComplexity.TMData.Accepts` with it dropped, so winning becomes the
715:  least fixed point of the game operator – an inductive predicate
716:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.ATMData.AltWin`), agreeing with the budgeted
717:  definition over a finite configuration space
718:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.ATMData.altWin_iff_exists_altAcc`). The alternation is
719:  *unbounded*: `DescriptiveComplexity.ATMData.BlocksWellFormed` is dropped for
720:  `DescriptiveComplexity.ATMData.BlocksSplit`, which only asks that the two
721:  marks of `FirstOrder.Language.turingAlt 2` partition the states, so no second
722:  machine record and no restated transport lemma is needed. With no universal
723:  state the model is the space-bounded nondeterministic one
724:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.ATMData.altAcceptsSpace_true_iff_acceptsSpace`), so it
725:  is a conservative extension.
726:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.MachineAltSpace.Membership` –
727:  **`ATMAcceptSpace ∈ EXPTIME`**
728:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.atmAcceptSpace_mem_EXPTIME`), EXPTIME's first natural
729:  problem and the half of `APSPACE = EXPTIME` ([Chandra–Kozen–Stockmeyer
730:  1981][chandra1981alternation]) that this design reaches. The machine is a
731:  `DescriptiveComplexity.SOGameSpec` at the block with one variable for the
732:  state, one for the head and one – binary – for the tape; its `move` sentence
733:  is `DescriptiveComplexity.TMData.Step` with seven elements of the *base*
734:  quantified (the transition, the two states, the two head positions, the symbol
735:  read and the symbol written) and one universal pair for the cells the head
736:  does not touch, so nothing quantifies over a configuration and the sentence is
737:  first-order over the base. The correspondence with
738:  `DescriptiveComplexity.ATMData.AltWin` is a bisimulation between two
739:  inductives of the same shape, needing only *a move lands on a configuration*
740:  and *a start is a configuration*, so the block's junk assignments are never
741:  reached. The two promises `DescriptiveComplexity.TMData.WellFormed` and
742:  `DescriptiveComplexity.ATMData.BlocksSplit` ride on the `start` sentence:
743:  `DescriptiveComplexity.ExpDefinable` compares `P A` with `Q (X.Map A)` and has
744:  nowhere else to put a condition on `A` alone.
745:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Exponential.GameInterp` – **`ATMAcceptSpace` is
746:  EXPTIME-complete** (`DescriptiveComplexity.atmAcceptSpace_EXPTIME_complete`),
747:  i.e., **`APSPACE = EXPTIME`** ([Chandra–Kozen–Stockmeyer
748:  1981][chandra1981alternation]): an alternating machine given as much space as
749:  its input has positions decides exactly the problems of deterministic
750:  exponential time. Hardness is a machine *written* by the reduction, from
751:  `EXPTIME = SO-GAME`: the tape holds two assignments of the game's block, cell
752:  by cell, and the control walks the six questions of the game
753:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.GameQuestion`) as quantifier prefixes, the existential
754:  player claiming the truth value of every block atom and the universal player
755:  challenging one of them – the challenge being *sought* on the tape, which is
756:  why no evaluator for arbitrary formulas is ever needed. The nine rule
757:  families and their walks are `DescriptiveComplexity.Exponential.GameMachine`;
758:  the simulation is `DescriptiveComplexity.altAcceptsSpace_iff_accepts`, forward
759:  in `DescriptiveComplexity.Exponential.GamePlay` and backwards in
760:  `DescriptiveComplexity.Exponential.GamePlayBack`, whose induction has to
761:  follow the universal sweep *forward* along a chain its motive quantifies over,
762:  a mid-sweep configuration having nothing true to say. The reduction is an
763:  ordinary ordered one, not a relativized one: the machine's `Posn` excludes the
764:  junk tuples by a relation rather than by the universe.
765:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.ReachabilityDet` – **REACHd is LOGSPACE-complete**
766:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.REACHd_LOGSPACE_complete`). The outdegree bound of the
767:  textbook statement is imposed semantically rather than as a promise: the walk
768:  follows an arc only when it is the only arc out of its source
769:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.DetEdge`), so every marked graph is a legal instance and
770:  invariance is free. Membership is `DescriptiveComplexity.reachSpec` read through its
771:  determinization; hardness reuses the FO(TC) interpretation verbatim, the graph
772:  of a determinized walk being functional, so that its forced arcs are all of
773:  its arcs. Both halves are cheaper than REACH's, whose membership needs
774:  Immerman–Szelepcsényi – the fragment asymmetry that forces it does not arise
775:  for an operator-based logic.
776:* `DescriptiveComplexity.HeadAutomaton` – **the machine model of the
777:  logarithmic-space level**, and the containment “machine ⊆ logic” for it. The
778:  model is a *two-way `k`-head automaton over the structure*: a finite control,
779:  `k` heads each holding an element of the universe, **no work tape**; a step
780:  reads the truth values of a fixed finite list of **quantifier-free** tests of
781:  the head positions (the `test_qf` field is what keeps the model a machine
782:  rather than first-order logic in disguise) and moves each head to the least or
783:  greatest element, to another head, or to the immediate successor or
784:  predecessor of another head – a head at the last element moving right having
785:  no successor, so the transition is disabled, as in
786:  `DescriptiveComplexity.TMData`. It is deliberately *not* a one-way `DFA`/`NFA` over
787:  an alphabet: the input is a structure and not a word, so such a machine would
788:  have to be given a serialization, and one-way single-head machines recognize
789:  only regular languages – the two-wayness and the `k` heads *are* the
790:  logarithmic-space bound. A configuration is a control state with a `k`-tuple,
791:  which is exactly a `DescriptiveComplexity.TCSpec.Node`, so an automaton compiles
792:  into a specification whose modes are its states
793:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.HeadAutomaton.toSpec`), whence
794:  `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NL_of_automaton` and, for a deterministic control,
795:  `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_LOGSPACE_of_automaton`.
796:* `DescriptiveComplexity.HeadProgram` – **the assembly language of those
797:  machines**: the same model with its transitions presented one at a time, each
798:  with its own quantifier-free guard and with two *exits*, so that machines can
799:  be pasted together. A fragment's specification is
800:  `DescriptiveComplexity.HeadProgram.Runs` – which exits are reachable, with which
801:  head positions – split into an exact soundness half and a completeness half
802:  that is up to the *scratch* heads, the ones a fragment may leave dirty.
803:  Everything is built with one combinator,
804:  `DescriptiveComplexity.HeadProgram.wireP`: a finite family of fragments, one per
805:  node of a control graph. `DescriptiveComplexity.HeadProgram.runs_wireP` reduces the
806:  runs of the assembly to a *walk in the control graph* whose steps are the runs
807:  of the fragments, which is what every correctness proof downstream argues
808:  about; its engine is
809:  `DescriptiveComplexity.HeadProgram.Embeds.reach_cases`, that a run which starts
810:  inside a fragment either is still inside it or has left it by one of its
811:  exits. Two compilations back to `DescriptiveComplexity.HeadAutomaton` enable either
812:  every transition whose guard holds or only the first, the latter being
813:  syntactically deterministic whatever the guards.
814:* `DescriptiveComplexity.HeadEval` – **a machine can decide any fixed first-order
815:  formula of its head positions** (`DescriptiveComplexity.HeadProgram.decides_evalP`),
816:  by structural recursion on the formula: atoms are guards, implication is a
817:  branch, and a quantifier is a *sweep* of two fresh heads – one walking the
818:  order from the least element, one parked at the greatest so that “the sweep is
819:  over” is the atom “these two heads are equal”. Quantifiers are thus not read
820:  but walked, which is why quantifier-free guards cost nothing in expressive
821:  power, and the sweep is deterministic
822:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.HeadProgram.deterministic_evalP`).
823:* `DescriptiveComplexity.HeadCapture` – **the capture theorem for NL**
824:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.tcDefinable_iff_automaton`,
825:  `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NL_iff_automaton`): every FO(TC) definable problem is
826:  recognized by a two-way multi-head automaton, so the machine model and the
827:  logic define the same class. The machine keeps the walk's current tuple on one
828:  block of heads and a candidate on another, holds the *mode* in its control –
829:  where it must be, a one-element universe having only one tuple – and loops:
830:  guess a source, evaluate the target formula, else guess a candidate, evaluate
831:  the transition formula, commit. Guessing (a head walked up the order for a
832:  nondeterministic number of steps) is the only nondeterminism. Soundness is an
833:  invariant carried along the control walk – the current tuple is a node
834:  reachable from a source – and completeness an induction along
835:  `DescriptiveComplexity.TCSpec.Reach`.
836:* `DescriptiveComplexity.HeadCaptureDet` – **the capture theorem for L**
837:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.dtcDefinable_iff_automaton`,
838:  `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_LOGSPACE_iff_automaton`): the same statement for FO(DTC)
839:  and *deterministic* machines. A deterministic machine may not guess, so it
840:  **searches** – the candidate tuple, the source tuple and the counter are each
841:  a block of heads walked by the odometer of `DescriptiveComplexity.HeadLex`
842:  (`lexNextP`, the lexicographic successor of a block, tested against a head
843:  parked at the greatest element, since maximality of one head is not a
844:  quantifier-free fact) – and it **counts**, so that a walk leading nowhere is
845:  abandoned rather than followed around its cycle for ever. The budget is
846:  `DescriptiveComplexity.WalkBudget`: a node reachable along a *functional* relation
847:  is reachable in fewer steps than the type has elements, and a counter in a
848:  finite linear order can tick as often as its rank leaves room. The two meet
849:  because the machine's counter – a mode in the control above a tuple on a block –
850:  *is* a finite linear order, whose covers are exactly its ticks and which has
851:  exactly as many values as the specification has nodes. Soundness is again an
852:  invariant along the control walk; completeness is the walk (an induction on the
853:  steps left, on the budget) inside the source enumeration (an induction
854:  downwards along the same order, the walk lemma supplying the return to the next
855:  source when one leads nowhere).
856:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.ReachabilityDet.Complement` – **`L = coL`**
857:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.LOGSPACE_eq_coLOGSPACE`) and **UNREACHd is
858:  LOGSPACE-complete** (`DescriptiveComplexity.UNREACHd_LOGSPACE_complete`). Everything
859:  rests on one membership statement: the complement of REACHd is itself a
860:  deterministic walk, which *scans* – it tries each vertex as a source in the
861:  order of the structure, following forced arcs from it with a budget, and
862:  accepts once the candidates are exhausted. The budget is a third coordinate
863:  holding a vertex, read through `DescriptiveComplexity.orank`, and it replaces cycle
864:  detection: a walk that has not arrived after `|A| - 1` steps never will, since
865:  a minimal number of steps visits distinct vertices
866:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.exists_iterate_lt_card`). The scan quantifies the sources
867:  itself because acceptance quantifies the *start* node existentially while a
868:  complement needs them universally. Given that one problem, closure of the
869:  class under complement is free: a reduction complements along with its two
870:  problems, and REACHd is hard.
871:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.TwoSat` – **2SAT is NL-complete**
872:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.TwoSAT_NL_complete`), the NL-level analogue of HORN-SAT for
873:  PTIME. A member by a Krom program that guesses the truth assignment and reads
874:  each clause through a covering pair of occurrences, enforcing the width
875:  promise and the absence of an empty clause by *guards* – first-order over the
876:  input, so a promise costs one goal clause; NL-hard by the Krom discharge,
877:  which emits one propositional 2-clause per clause of the program and per
878:  instantiation satisfying its guard, the output being width-two by
879:  construction. The scaffolding shared with the Horn discharge (dimension,
880:  tags, guard and atom-occurrence formulas over the canonical padding) is
881:  `DescriptiveComplexity.ClauseDischarge`. 2SAT is *also* in PTIME
882:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.twoSat_mem_PTIME`), by a Horn program guessing reachability
883:  in the implication graph of the 2-clauses and rejecting a variable that
884:  reaches its own negation and back – the classical criterion of [Aspvall,
885:  Plass & Tarjan 1979][aspvall1979linear], formalized in
886:  `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.TwoSat.Implication`; this is what yields the two
887:  inclusions of NL.
888:

 succeeded in 10854ms:
1564:## Value invention, towards the recursively enumerable
1565:
1566:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNew` – `∃SO[new]`, existential second-order
1567:  logic whose relation variables range over the universe *extended by finitely
1568:  many invented values*, in the style of the object-creating query languages of
1569:  ([Abiteboul–Hull–Vianu 1995][abiteboul1995foundations], ch. 18). Every other
1570:  logic here bounds its certificate by the instance – a `Σ₁` sentence guesses
1571:  relations over `A`, so the search space is exponential in `|A|` and the class
1572:  sits inside NP. Value invention removes that bound and nothing else: the
1573:  certificate is a finite extension `A ⊕ Fin m` with `m` unbounded, together
1574:  with relations over it, checked by a fixed first-order kernel over the base
1575:  vocabulary plus one predicate `old` marking the original elements. A witness
1576:  is still finite and the kernel still decidable on it, so definability in this
1577:  logic is a machine-model-free reading of *recursive enumerability*.
1578:  `DescriptiveComplexity.SigmaSODefinable.toNew` is `Σ₁ ⊆ ∃SO[new]`, by
1579:  inventing nothing.
1580:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewBdd` – **value invention, bounded**:
1581:  `DescriptiveComplexity.SigmaSONewBddDefinable` is the same logic with the
1582:  number of invented values held to `Nat.card (Fin d → A)`, as many as the
1583:  instance has `d`-tuples. The point of the parameter is that the bound hands
1584:  the search space back to the instance, so the family reads *invent nothing*
1585:  (`Σ₁`), *invent polynomially many*, *invent exponentially many* and *invent
1586:  unboundedly many* (RE) as one definition. Note that the notions are not
1587:  weakenings of one another – a definability statement is an equivalence, so
1588:  moving the bound costs the sentence a re-guarding, not merely a relaxation;
1589:  `DescriptiveComplexity.SigmaSODefinable.toNewBdd` is the inclusion `Σ₁ ⊆
1590:  ∃SO[new, d]`, again by inventing nothing.
1591:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewBddPull` – the converse, and with it
1592:  **`∃SO[new, d] = NP`**
1593:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.sigmaSONewBddDefinable_iff_sigmaSODefinable`). A
1594:  bounded extension is the universe of a *relativized* interpretation of the
1595:  instance: two tags and dimension `d`, an original element on the diagonal and
1596:  an invented value wherever a **guessed** `d`-ary relation puts it. Their number
1597:  is then at most the number of `d`-tuples whatever the guess, and reaches every
1598:  value the bound allows for a suitable one, so the `∃ m` of the definition
1599:  becomes the block's `∃ N`. This is what the bound is for: an interpretation
1600:  cannot invent, so the values have to come from the instance.
1601:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewExp` – the expansion a bounded invention
1602:  lives in, and the library's first concrete
1603:  `DescriptiveComplexity.ExpExpansion`: two tags over a block of one `d`-ary and
1604:  one unary variable, an *original* point naming one element and inventing
1605:  nothing, a *new* point naming none. Its universe is the instance's elements
1606:  together with its `d`-ary relations
1607:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.powPointEquiv`), so it holds `n + 2 ^ nᵈ` points –
1608:  enough for any extension `DescriptiveComplexity.SigmaSONewExpDefinable`
1609:  allows – its block is `c` variables of arity `d`, so its new points number
1610:  `2 ^ (c · nᵈ)`, two constants and not one because at a one-element instance
1611:  `nᵈ` is `1` whatever `d` is. Its vocabulary is
1612:  `DescriptiveComplexity.newLang L`, so what the
1613:  expanded structure is, is the extended structure with every invented value
1614:  present: `DescriptiveComplexity.powExtEquiv` is that isomorphism, carried by
1615:  `DescriptiveComplexity.extOn`, the extended structure over an arbitrary set of
1616:  invented values (`DescriptiveComplexity.extStructure` being its `Fin m` case).
1617:  A sentence that wants fewer values marks the ones it uses, which is a guess
1618:  and so stays inside `Σ₁`, and `DescriptiveComplexity.usedSubEquiv` says what
1619:  the marking buys: the substructure on the original elements together with the
1620:  marked values *is* the extension by those values alone. What comes out is
1621:  `DescriptiveComplexity.SigmaSONewExpDefinable.toExpDefinable`, **`∃SO[new,
1622:  exp c d] ⊆ NEXPTIME`**: a definition that invents at most as many values as
1623:  the instance has tuples of `c` relations of arity `d` is a `Σ₁` definition
1624:  over the expansion, the `∃ m` of the bound becoming the guess of a unary
1625:  marker.
1626:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewCount` – **surjectivity from a flip**.
1627:  A sentence can say that a guessed family of sets contains the empty one, is
1628:  closed under flipping a single element, and is injectively indexed; it cannot
1629:  say that the family is *onto*, quantifying over all sets being second order.
1630:  `DescriptiveComplexity.eq_of_flipClosed` buys that anyway, in Lean rather than
1631:  in the logic: a flip-closed family containing the empty set is everything, so
1632:  an injective guess into it is a bijection
1633:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.bijective_of_flipClosedP`). This is where the bound of
1634:  an exponentially-bounded invention is spent.
1635:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewMeans` – **what the invented values
1636:  mean**. To read a problem over an exponential expansion as one with value
1637:  invention, the invented values have to *be* the expansion's points, and a
1638:  point is a relation over the instance; so the sentence guesses a *meaning
1639:  relation* with one more argument, `M v x⃗` saying that `v` names a relation
1640:  holding of `x⃗`. Three of its four guards are ordinary first-order statements –
1641:  the relation is shaped (invented value to original elements), injective, and
1642:  the empty relation is named – and the fourth,
1643:  `DescriptiveComplexity.meanFlip`, is what makes the guess *onto*: every named
1644:  relation with one tuple flipped is named too.
1645:  `DescriptiveComplexity.bijective_meanAt_of_guard` cashes them, through the
1646:  counting of `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewCount`, into a bijection
1647:  between the invented values and the relations of the instance.
1648:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewMeansB` – the same for a whole **block**,
1649:  which is what a point of an expansion actually is: one meaning relation per
1650:  variable, of that variable's arity plus one, with the four guards taken
1651:  variable by variable and the flip leaving the other variables alone. An
1652:  assignment of a block is a set of `Σ i, Fin (B.arity i) → A` – a tuple tagged
1653:  by the variable it belongs to – so flips of that one sigma type are exactly
1654:  flips of one tuple of one variable, and
1655:  `DescriptiveComplexity.bijective_meanAtB_of_guard` reads the guards as a
1656:  bijection between the invented values and *all* assignments of the block. A
1657:  value carries its **tag** the same way, with no machinery of its own: add one
1658:  nullary variable per tag to the block, and the meaning relation of a nullary
1659:  variable is unary, `M v`, read as “the value `v` carries this tag”
1660:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.consTagAssignEquiv`).
1661:* `DescriptiveComplexity.ParamFormula` – **vocabulary maps with parameters**.
1662:  An `FirstOrder.Language.LHom` keeps a symbol's arity, so it cannot say “read
1663:  this symbol at a value the formula holds in a variable” – which is what a
1664:  translation through the meaning relations has to do, a meaning being one
1665:  relation of arity one more indexed by the value it belongs to. A
1666:  `DescriptiveComplexity.ParamHom` gives each source symbol a number of
1667:  parameter variables and a target symbol of that much larger arity, and
1668:  `DescriptiveComplexity.ParamHom.realize_onSentenceF` reads the image in the
1669:  target structure as the source read in the structure the parameters' values
1670:  induce. Symbols with no parameter are the ordinary renaming, so one map can
1671:  carry the base vocabulary through untouched while the block symbols pick up
1672:  an index. The parameters are values the *marked part* of the target need not
1673:  contain, so `DescriptiveComplexity.relativizeTo` cannot be applied on its own
1674:  – its correctness moves the whole formula into a substructure, where an atom
1675:  holding a parameter has no reading at all;
1676:  `DescriptiveComplexity.ParamHom.realize_relOnSentenceF` is the two steps
1677:  taken together, the quantifiers guarded by the marker and the symbols still
1678:  mentioning the parameters.
1679:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SubstFormula` – **interpreting a vocabulary by
1680:  formulas on a definable part**. An `DescriptiveComplexity.FOInterpretation`
1681:  builds its universe out of tagged `d`-tuples, which a translation reading one
1682:  element per point pays for without using;
1683:  `DescriptiveComplexity.FormulaSubst` gives one formula per relation symbol
1684:  instead, and `DescriptiveComplexity.FormulaSubst.substTo` substitutes them
1685:  while guarding every quantifier by a domain formula
1686:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.FormulaSubst.realize_substTo`). The definable part is
1687:  an arbitrary type with an injection into the target whose range the domain
1688:  formula defines, not a subtype, so a caller can take it to be the object it
1689:  already has – the universe of an expansion, say.
1690:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewRead` – **reading an expansion's
1691:  defining sentences through the meanings**. A sentence defining a relation of
1692:  an expanded vocabulary is written over the ordered base vocabulary expanded by
1693:  one copy of the block per argument; value invention holds those arguments as
1694:  invented values of one extended universe. So the sentence is read with its
1695:  base symbols passing through but among the original elements only, its order
1696:  symbol at a *guessed* order, and the block symbol of copy `i` at the meaning
1697:  relation of its variable, applied to the value copy `i` holds
1698:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.readHom`, a `DescriptiveComplexity.ParamHom`).
1699:  `DescriptiveComplexity.realize_readHom` is what that is worth: the structure
1700:  the map induces on the original elements *is* the base structure expanded by
1701:  the copies of the block, interpreted by the assignments the values mean. The
1702:  target vocabulary stays abstract – a `DescriptiveComplexity.ReadSyms` names
1703:  only the symbols used – so the assembly is free to place them.
1704:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewPoint` – **which invented values are
1705:  points**, and what the expanded relations say of them. An invented value
1706:  carries an assignment (through the meanings) and a tag (through the nullary
1707:  variables); it is a *point* when it carries exactly one tag and its assignment
1708:  satisfies that tag's domain sentence, which is
1709:  `DescriptiveComplexity.isPointF`. `DescriptiveComplexity.pointRelF` is the
1710:  atom of the expanded vocabulary: one disjunct per tuple of tags, guarded by
1711:  the tag symbols of the values, whose body is the defining sentence at that
1712:  tuple read through the meanings. Everywhere else in the library a tag is
1713:  chosen when the formula is built; here they are guessed, so the formula
1714:  carries a disjunct for each of the finitely many tuples.
1715:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewExpPull` – **the block a problem over an
1716:  expansion is guessed in**. Everything the rewritten sentence guesses goes into
1717:  one second-order block: the order on the original elements (so the block is a
1718:  `DescriptiveComplexity.SOBlock.withOrder`, guarded by
1719:  `DescriptiveComplexity.extLinearGuard`), the meanings of the expansion's block
1720:  and of the tags, and the source problem's own `Σ₁` block, whose variables
1721:  range over the points and so are guessed over the extended universe.
1722:  `DescriptiveComplexity.pullPointOn` reads an assignment of that block as the
1723:  data the translations ask for, and `DescriptiveComplexity.realize_pullKernel`
1724:  is the kernel: the source problem's first-order kernel, with
1725:  `DescriptiveComplexity.pointRelF` for the atoms of the expanded vocabulary and
1726:  “is a point” as the domain formula, holds in the extended universe exactly
1727:  when it holds over the expansion.
1728:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewExpBuild` – **the guess the forward
1729:  direction makes**: one invented value per assignment of the tagged block, the
1730:  meaning variables saying which tuples belong to it, the order variable the
1731:  instance's order, and the source problem's variables the certificate read at
1732:  the values naming the points. Every guard is checked against it, and
1733:  `DescriptiveComplexity.card_taggedAssign_le` counts what it invents.
1734:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewExpConv` – **`∃SO[new, exp] = NEXPTIME`**
1735:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NEXPTIME_iff_sigmaSONewExpDefinable`). The two
1736:  constants are the expansion's – how many variables its block has once one
1737:  nullary variable per tag is added, and how wide they are – so no single pair
1738:  serves every problem and they are quantified.
1739:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Relativize` – relativization of a formula to a unary
1740:  predicate (`DescriptiveComplexity.relativizeTo`), with its correctness against
1741:  the substructure the predicate defines. Its instance here is
1742:  `DescriptiveComplexity.relOld`: a formula about the instance, read in the
1743:  extended universe with its quantifiers restricted to the original elements,
1744:  says what it says in the instance.
1745:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewPull` – **`∃SO[new]` definability is
1746:  closed under FO reductions** (`DescriptiveComplexity.SigmaSONewDefinable.of_foReduction`).
1747:  The construction is the one value invention makes cheap: with the *same*
1748:  number of invented values, the target's extended universe `I.Map A ⊕ Fin m` is
1749:  **definable inside** the source's `A ⊕ Fin m` – an interpreted point is a tag
1750:  with `dim` original coordinates, an invented value is itself – so it is the
1751:  universe of a relativized interpretation with tags `Tag ⊕ Unit` and dimension
1752:  `dim + 1`, and the kernel is pulled back through it by the guarded pullback of
1753:  `DescriptiveComplexity.RelComposition`. The spare coordinate is pinned to a
1754:  guessed canonical element, which is what makes the construction survive
1755:  `dim = 0`.
1756:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderNewOrdered` – the same closure under
1757:  *ordered* FO reductions: the order is re-quantified inside the block, guarded
1758:  by `DescriptiveComplexity.extLinearGuard`, which must be **relativized** –
1759:  the order symbol of an extended structure relates original elements only, so
1760:  an unrelativized linear-order guard would be unsatisfiable as soon as
1761:  something is invented.
1762:* `DescriptiveComplexity.RecursivelyEnumerable` – **the class RE**
1763:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.RE`), a `DescriptiveComplexity.ComplexityClass` by
1764:  those two closures, with `NP ⊆ RE` (`DescriptiveComplexity.NP_subset_RE`) and
1765:  the complement operator `DescriptiveComplexity.coRE`. `∃SO[new]` has no dual
1766:  reading, so nothing in that file relates RE and co-RE; the separation
1767:  `DescriptiveComplexity.RE_ne_coRE` is proved where the class meets Mathlib's
1768:  computability layer, in
1769:  `DescriptiveComplexity.Computability.CodeHaltComplete`. Its first complete
1770:  problem is finite satisfiability, by Trakhtenbrot's theorem
1771:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.FinSat`), and Post's correspondence problem
1772:  is a member of it (`DescriptiveComplexity.pcp_mem_RE`).
1773:
1774:## Shared encodings
1775:
1776:* `DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderMerge` – merging a second-order quantifier
1777:  prefix into a single block (and back), so that constructions stated for one
1778:  block can read the kernel of a `k`-block sentence.
1779:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Padding` – canonically padded tuples: the convention
1780:  by which a single interpretation dimension can carry tuples of different
1781:  lengths (pad with a minimum of the input order), together with the FO(≤)
1782:  formulas expressing it. This is the one place where the SAT-family
1783:  reductions need their input to be ordered.
1784:* `DescriptiveComplexity.EqPattern` – data read only through its **equality
1785:  pattern** (which coordinates hold the least element, which the greatest,
1786:  which two are equal) is first-order definable, by one formula for every
1787:  structure. The pattern type is finite, so the formula is the disjunction of
1788:  the patterns admitted. This is what lets a machine assembled rule by rule be
1789:  written down as an interpretation without threading syntax through every
1790:  abstraction it is built from: a rule owes a `Prop` about its guard where the
1791:  guard is defined, not a formula. The write side is the same idea one step on:
1792:  `DescriptiveComplexity.SlotVal` names each output coordinate as a copy of an
1793:  input one, one of the two designated elements, or the **next** element after
1794:  an input one (`DescriptiveComplexity.ordSucc`, the cover in a finite linear
1795:  order), and `DescriptiveComplexity.writeTupF` is the formula that says a
1796:  tuple was written that way.
1797:* `DescriptiveComplexity.OccurrenceOrder` and
1798:  `DescriptiveComplexity.OccurrenceFormulas` – machinery for encoding
1799:  occurrences of literals in clauses, shared across the SAT-family reductions.
1800:* `DescriptiveComplexity.OrderWalk` – walking a finite linear order (or the
1801:  lexicographic order on tuples) first-order: min/max/successor guards and
1802:  their tuple analogues, induction along covers, and the rank of an element.
1803:  Shared between the HORN-SAT program, the FO(LFP) → SO-Horn translation and
1804:  the counting machine, whose registers are exactly ranks and tuple walks.
1805:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Numbers` – unary and binary encodings of numbers as
1806:  finite structures, for threshold and weight parameters of problems; its
1807:  module docstring argues the per-problem choice between the two.
1808:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Machines` – Turing machines as relations on a
1809:  universe, with no vocabulary: configurations, steps, and acceptance within a
1810:  budget counted in universe elements. The semantics the machine bridge reads
1811:  off an instance.
1812:
1813:## The bridge to Mathlib's computability layer
1814:
1815:Every class of this development is defined by a *logic*, and every problem is
1816:an isomorphism-closed property of finite structures. `ComputablePred` and
1817:`REPred`, on the other hand, are predicates on a `Primcodable` type, so
1818:relating the two needs a passage from isomorphism classes to data. It is built
1819:once for the catalog rather than once per problem.
1820:
1821:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Computability` – the umbrella. A finite structure over
1822:  a finitely presented relational vocabulary becomes a universe `Fin (n + 1)`
1823:  and a list of Boolean tables (`FirstOrder.Language.FinStruct`, a
1824:  `Primcodable` type, nonempty and linearly ordered by construction); a fixed
1825:  first-order formula is evaluated on it *primitive recursively*
1826:  (`FirstOrder.Language.FinStruct.primrec_evalBF`), and hence decidably on any
1827:  finite structure at all (`FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula.decidableRealize`
1828:  – the first formal justification of the claim, elsewhere by inspection, that
1829:  first-order interpretations are effective).
1830:* `DescriptiveComplexity.RE_subset_rePred` – **RE really is recursively
1831:  enumerable**: the `∃SO[new]` certificate, a number of invented values and an
1832:  assignment of the relation variables, is a finite object, so it is *searched
1833:  for*, and the first-order kernel is checked on it by the evaluator. This makes
1834:  the name of the class a theorem rather than a convention, and it needs no
1835:  machine model. Read at the two problems of the machine bridge, it gives
1836:  `DescriptiveComplexity.halt_rePred` and
1837:  `DescriptiveComplexity.finsat_rePred`.
1838:
1839:* `DescriptiveComplexity.not_computablePred_of_relOrderedReduction` – **first-order
1840:  reductions are computable**: an interpretation induces a computable many-one
1841:  reduction of the induced sets, so undecidability transfers backwards along
1842:  `≤ᶠᵒ`, `≤ᶠᵒ[≤]` and `≤ʳᶠᵒ[≤]`. The order costs nothing (the universe of a
1843:  concrete instance is already `Fin (n + 1)`); the work is the *renumbering* a
1844:  definable target domain forces, and the run-time choice among the `|Tag|ⁿ`
1845:  instances of a defining formula.
1846:
1847:* `DescriptiveComplexity.not_computablePred_codehalt` – **the first problem of
1848:  the catalog proved undecidable outright**. Mathlib's halting problem is
1849:  carried in by making the *code the instance*: a `Nat.Partrec.Code` is drawn
1850:  as its syntax tree (`DescriptiveComplexity.CODEHALT`,
1851:  `DescriptiveComplexity.codeStruct`), so the map from codes to instances is a
1852:  plain tree flattening and hence primitive recursive – which the simulation of
1853:  a machine could not be, Mathlib's universal machine not being finite-state.
1854:
1855:* `DescriptiveComplexity.not_computablePred_of_RE_hard` – **an RE-hard problem
1856:  is undecidable**, once and for all. Hardness here is cofinal, so an RE-hard
1857:  problem is in particular a target of CODEHALT, which is undecidable, and the
1858:  reduction is computable. This is the leverage the layer exists for: a
1859:  completeness theorem for RE now yields undecidability with no computability
1860:  work of its own. Its first instance is
1861:  `DescriptiveComplexity.finsat_not_computable`, **Trakhtenbrot's theorem**:
1862:  whether a first-order sentence has a *finite* model is undecidable.
1863:
1864:* `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_RE_iff_rePred` – **RE is exactly recursive
1865:  enumerability**, the converse inclusion and with it the identity of the
1866:  logically defined class with the machine one. A semi-decidable problem
1867:  reduces to CODEHALT by drawing the instance as the *program* that runs a
1868:  semi-decision procedure on it: the procedure is
1869:  *obtained* from Mathlib (`Nat.Partrec.Code.exists_code`) rather than built,
1870:  which is exactly what spares the layer the evaluator with addressed storage
1871:  a machine target would need. Whence
1872:  `DescriptiveComplexity.codehalt_RE_complete` and, by Post's theorem applied
1873:  to the undecidability above, `DescriptiveComplexity.RE_ne_coRE`.
1874:

 succeeded in 14586ms:
1875:## The problem catalog
1876:
1877:`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems` holds one decision problem per file, each with
1878:its vocabulary, FO reductions and a completeness theorem. Every class in the
1879:table below is *defined* logically; each problem listed is proved **complete**
1880:for it – both a member and hard under FO reductions. The catalog covers all of
1881:Karp's 21 NP-complete problems. Each problem's own module page documents its
1882:reduction and certificate in full.
1883:
1884:| Complexity class | Logical characterization | Machine model | Problems proved complete |
1885:| --- | --- | --- | --- |
1886:| `LOGSPACE` (`L`) | FO(≤, DTC): first-order logic with a deterministic transitive closure, over a linearly ordered universe | deterministic two-way `k`-head automaton † | REACHd · UNREACHd |
1887:| `NL` | SO-Krom(≤): ∃SO with a Krom kernel, at most two second-order literals per clause; equivalently FO(≤, TC), first-order logic with a transitive closure – both over a linearly ordered universe | two-way `k`-head automaton † | REACH · UNREACH · 2SAT |
1888:| `PTIME` = `Σ₀ᵖ` = `Π₀ᵖ` | SO-Horn(≤): ∃SO with a Horn kernel; equivalently FO(≤, LFP), first-order logic with a least fixed point – both over a linearly ordered universe | deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine | HORN-SAT · CVP |
1889:| `NP` = `Σ₁ᵖ` | ∃SO: existential second-order logic | nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machine | **SAT-family:** SAT · 3SAT · NAE-SAT · NAE-3SAT · 1-in-SAT<br>**Coloring:** 3-Colorability · `k`-Colorability (`k ≥ 3`) · Chromatic Number · Clique Cover<br>**Cliques & subgraphs:** Clique · Independent Set · Vertex Cover · Subgraph Isomorphism<br>**Sets & hypergraphs:** Set Cover · Hitting Set · Set Packing · Exact Cover · Set Splitting · Dominating Set · 3-Dimensional Matching<br>**Graphs:** Feedback Vertex Set · Feedback Arc Set · Steiner Tree (node- & edge-weighted) · Max Cut · Hamilton Circuit (directed & undirected)<br>**Numbers (in binary):** Knapsack · Partition · 0-1 Integer Programming · Job Sequencing<br>**Machines:** acceptance by a nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machine |
1890:| `coNP` = `Π₁ᵖ` | ∀SO: universal second-order logic | the same machine, accepting when *every* run does | TAUT · 3-DNF-TAUT · 3-UNSAT (and QBF∀ at one block) · `ATMAccept 1 false` |
1891:| `DP` | a `Σ₁` and a `Π₁` sentence conjoined | — | SAT-UNSAT |
1892:| `Σₖᵖ` (`k ≥ 1`) | `Σₖ¹`: `k` alternating second-order quantifier blocks, existential first | alternating polynomial-time Turing machine, `k` blocks, existential first | `QBF k` – at `k = 1`, NP · `ATMAccept k true` |
1893:| `Πₖᵖ` (`k ≥ 1`) | `Πₖ¹`: `k` alternating second-order quantifier blocks, universal first | the same machine, universal first | `QBF∀ k` – at `k = 1`, coNP · `ATMAccept k false` |
1894:| `PH` | full second-order logic | — | — |
1895:| `PSPACE` | SO(TC): second-order logic with a transitive closure over assignments of a block of relation variables | polynomial-space Turing machine, deterministic or not | SUCCINCT-REACH · QSAT · space-bounded machine acceptance (deterministic & not) |
1896:| `EXPTIME` | SO(LFP): PTIME read over an exponential expansion; equivalently SO-GAME, a second-order alternating game | alternating polynomial-space Turing machine | acceptance by such a machine (`APSPACE = EXPTIME`) |
1897:| `NEXPTIME` | ∃SO over an exponential expansion, i.e., NP read there; equivalently ∃SO[new, exp], value invention bounded exponentially | wide machine, clocked | acceptance by such a machine within its clock · tiling a wide square (the `2ⁿ × 2ⁿ` tiling) |
1898:| `EXPSPACE` | SO(PFP): PSPACE read over an exponential expansion | wide machine, space-bounded | acceptance by such a machine in bounded space (deterministic & not) · tiling a wide corridor (width `2ⁿ`, unbounded height) |
1899:| `RE` | ∃SO[new]: ∃SO with value invention, the relation variables ranging over the universe extended by finitely many invented values | Turing machine, no step or space bound | FINSAT (Trakhtenbrot's theorem) · CODEHALT · HALT · PCP (Post's correspondence problem) |
1900:| the degree of a problem: `DescriptiveComplexity.ComplexityClass.below Q₀`, e.g., `GI` | none – a downward closure under `≤ᶠᵒ[≤]` rather than a logic, which is the point of the construction | — | for `GI`: Graph Isomorphism · Digraph Isomorphism · DAG Isomorphism |
1901:
1902:Two of the models are named rather than described: both head automata walk a
1903:linear order of the universe, and a *wide* machine carries its control in the
1904:instance while its tape is addressed by an exponential expansion of it
1905:(`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Wide`).
1906:
1907:Each entry of the **machine model** column is an equivalence *proved here*
1908:between the logical definition of the class and acceptance by that model:
1909:`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_LOGSPACE_iff_automaton` and
1910:`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NL_iff_automaton` (†), and, through the completeness
1911:of an acceptance problem, `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_PTIME_iff_le_dtmAccept`,
1912:`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NP_iff_le_ntmAccept`,
1913:`DescriptiveComplexity.le_dtmAcceptSpace_of_mem_PSPACE`,
1914:`DescriptiveComplexity.atmAcceptSpace_EXPTIME_complete`,
1915:`DescriptiveComplexity.wideRegAccept_NEXPTIME_complete`,
1916:`DescriptiveComplexity.wideAcceptSpace_EXPSPACE_complete` and
1917:`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_RE_iff_rePred`. A dash marks a class for which no
1918:such equivalence is proved here.
1919:
1920:† Capture theorems, both directions: `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NL_iff_automaton`
1921:for `NL`, and `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_LOGSPACE_iff_automaton` for `LOGSPACE`,
1922:where the machine is required to be deterministic.
1923:
1924:Headline results and cross-references:
1925:
1926:* **Cook–Levin, machine-free** (`DescriptiveComplexity.SAT_NP_complete`;
1927:  [Cook 1971][cook1971complexity]; [Levin 1973][levin1973universal]): SAT is
1928:  NP-complete by a Tseitin discharge, no machine model. 3-colorability is
1929:  FO-interreducible with SAT in both directions.
1930:* **The machine bridge**: machine acceptance
1931:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.NTMAccept`) – does this nondeterministic Turing
1932:  machine, carried as data by the instance, accept its input within a
1933:  polynomial step budget (as many steps as there are tape positions)? – is
1934:  NP-complete
1935:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.ntmAccept_NP_complete`), so a problem is in the
1936:  library's NP exactly when it ordered-FO-reduces to it
1937:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NP_iff_le_ntmAccept`): the logically defined
1938:  class *is* the machine one. The textbook Cook–Levin – machine acceptance
1939:  reduces to SAT – is `DescriptiveComplexity.ntmAccept_reduces_to_sat`. One
1940:  level down, the *deterministic* restriction
1941:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.DTMAccept`, a functional transition table folded into
1942:  the yes-instances) is PTIME-complete
1943:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.dtmAccept_PTIME_complete`): membership because a
1944:  deterministic run is a least fixed point, read through the formalized
1945:  FO(LFP) → SO-Horn translation, and hardness by a unit-propagation machine
1946:  built inside the HORN-SAT instance – so PTIME, too, is the machine class
1947:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_PTIME_iff_le_dtmAccept`), with the Grädel-side
1948:  textbook discharge `DescriptiveComplexity.dtmAccept_reduces_to_hornSat`.
1949:* **The machine bridge for the hierarchy**: the same identification one level
1950:  of alternation at a time. `DescriptiveComplexity.ATMAccept k start` – does
1951:  this *alternating* machine, whose states carry `k` block marks entered in
1952:  order, accept its input within the same unary budget? – is `Σₖᵖ`-complete for
1953:  an existential first block
1954:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.atmAccept_sigmaP_complete`) and `Πₖᵖ`-complete for a
1955:  universal one (`DescriptiveComplexity.atmAccept_piP_complete`), so each level
1956:  of the logically defined hierarchy is the corresponding level of the
1957:  alternating-machine hierarchy of [Chandra–Kozen–Stockmeyer
1958:  1981][chandra1981alternation]. At one block the two are the nondeterministic
1959:  model and its dual, which is where coNP gets its machine
1960:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.atmAccept_one_complete`,
1961:  `DescriptiveComplexity.atmAccept_one_coNP_complete`,
1962:  `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_sigmaP_iff_le_atmAccept`,
1963:  `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_piP_iff_le_atmAccept`). Membership reads a run as
1964:  a `k`-round game, each round guessing one walk; hardness builds the machine
1965:  `M_φ` of a quantified Boolean formula inside the instance – one sweep of the
1966:  tape per quantifier block, whose only choice is which of its block's
1967:  variables to set, so that the moves of a round *are* the truth assignments of
1968:  its block, followed by a deterministic check phase walking the clauses.
1969:* **All of Karp's 21** ([Karp 1972][karp1972reducibility]): the SAT, clique,
1970:  set, coloring, graph and number families above, closed by the two Hamilton
1971:  circuit problems – a circuit read as a linear order of the universe, hard
1972:  from Vertex Cover by Karp's twelve-vertex cover-testing gadget.
1973:* **CVP, the textbook `PTIME`-complete problem**
1974:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.CVP_PTIME_complete`; [Ladner
1975:  1975][ladner1975circuit]): membership is an FO(LFP) definition – the problem's
1976:  semantics *is* a least fixed point, so the rule system is the gate rules
1977:  transcribed and the output sentence is the one a Horn program cannot write,
1978:  “the output gate is in the true rail”. Hardness draws the unit-propagation
1979:  circuit inside a HORN-SAT instance and reports the *failure* of Horn
1980:  satisfiability, which keeps the circuit monotone and costs nothing, polynomial
1981:  time being closed under complement. The stages of the fixed point are unrolled
1982:  along the order and the two unbounded quantifiers of a round become chains of
1983:  fan-in-two gates; what makes it work is that the *wiring*, being defined by a
1984:  formula, may test where a literal occurs, where a fixed circuit may not.
1985:* **PTIME by the Horn fragment**: HORN-SAT is PTIME-complete
1986:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.HORNSAT_PTIME_complete`) by the Horn discharge and a
1987:  Horn program for unit propagation – the P-level analogue of Cook–Levin,
1988:  equally machine-free. REACH/UNREACH is a second worked instance of the
1989:  fragment, and a third one of the Krom fragment:
1990:  `DescriptiveComplexity.unreach_mem_NL` defines UNREACH by a two-literal
1991:  program guessing the vertices from which a marked target is reachable. In
1992:  both fragments it is the *complement* that is definable head-on, clauses
1993:  being able to close and to reject but not to force minimality; REACH escapes
1994:  at the Horn level through FO(LFP), and at the Krom level through `NL = coNL`
1995:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.reach_mem_NL`).
1996:* **Immerman–Vardi, `PTIME = FO(≤, LFP)`**
1997:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.lfpDefinable_iff_mem_PTIME`; [Vardi
1998:  1982][vardi1982complexity]; [Immerman 1986][immerman1986relational]): a problem is
1999:  in polynomial time exactly when a least-fixed-point definition computes it over a
2000:  linearly ordered universe – order-*invariantly*, since
2001:  `DescriptiveComplexity.LFPDefinable` asks for the equivalence at every linear order.
2002:  The class being *defined* by the Horn fragment, the content is the pair of
2003:  translations of `DescriptiveComplexity.FixedPointHorn`, so the theorem is
2004:  machine-free like everything else here; the machine reading is the bridge
2005:  `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_PTIME_iff_le_dtmAccept`. The inflationary variant
2006:  `DescriptiveComplexity.ifpDefinable_iff_mem_PTIME` is the same statement for
2007:  FO(≤, IFP), and `DescriptiveComplexity.hornSat_hard_of_lfpDefinable` is the
2008:  hardness discharge from the logic – a hardness proof may start from a fixed-point
2009:  definition, where negation is free, rather than from a Horn program.
2010:* **L by deterministic transitive closure**: REACHd – reachability along
2011:  *forced* arcs – is complete for `DescriptiveComplexity.LOGSPACE`
2012:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.REACHd_LOGSPACE_complete`), the class defined by FO(DTC).
2013:  Determinism is carried by a formula rather than by a hypothesis, which is what
2014:  lets the class be closed under reductions syntactically; and both halves of
2015:  the completeness proof are the same observation read in opposite directions,
2016:  the graph of a deterministic walk being a deterministic-reachability instance
2017:  and conversely.
2018:* **`L = coL`, cheaply** (`DescriptiveComplexity.LOGSPACE_eq_coLOGSPACE`):
2019:  deterministic logarithmic space is closed under complement, and UNREACHd is
2020:  complete for it. Where `NL = coNL` needs Immerman–Szelepcsényi's inductive
2021:  counting, a *deterministic* walk has only one thing to do at each node, so
2022:  failing to arrive is witnessed by walking until a budget runs out – and the
2023:  budget is just a vertex, counted by its rank in the order.
2024:* **NL by the Krom fragment and FO(TC)**: 2SAT is NL-complete
2025:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.TwoSAT_NL_complete`) by the Krom discharge, and so is
2026:  REACH (`DescriptiveComplexity.REACH_NL_complete`), the canonical NL-complete
2027:  problem ([Jones 1975][jones1975space]), whose hardness is the FO(TC)
2028:  discharge – the interpretation *is* the graph of the walk of a
2029:  `DescriptiveComplexity.TCSpec`. Both halves of REACH's completeness pass
2030:  through Immerman–Szelepcsényi: membership because a clausal fragment defines
2031:  only non-reachability, hardness because SO-Krom definability has to be turned
2032:  into an FO(TC) definition of the problem itself. UNREACH is then complete as
2033:  well (`DescriptiveComplexity.UNREACH_NL_complete`), the two problems trading
2034:  which half is the easy one.
2035:* **The logarithmic-space machine model, captured**
2036:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NL_iff_automaton`,
2037:  `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_LOGSPACE_iff_automaton`): a problem is in `NL` exactly
2038:  when a two-way `k`-head automaton over the structure recognizes it, and in
2039:  `LOGSPACE` exactly when a *deterministic* one does. There is no string
2040:  encoding anywhere: the machine reads the structure through quantifier-free
2041:  tests of its heads, and `k` head positions are the `k · log n` bits of
2042:  storage. The logic-to-machine half is a compiler – quantifiers are *walked*
2043:  by a two-head sweep rather than read – and its deterministic version is the
2044:  same machine with search in place of guessing and a step budget in place of
2045:  an oracle: the counter is a mode above a tuple, one finite linear order with
2046:  exactly as many values as the specification has nodes.
2047:* **Above NP**: TAUT (DNF tautology) is coNP-complete by complementing the
2048:  Cook–Levin discharge, and its width-three restriction 3-DNF-TAUT
2049:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.ThreeDnfTAUT_coNP_complete`) follows the same route
2050:  through the CNF-side reading 3-UNSAT, which is where the width promise of the
2051:  clause-splitting reduction is still in hand (`3SATᶜ` would not do: it is a
2052:  disjunction, since 3SAT folds the width bound into its yes-instances);
2053:  `QBF k`, quantified Boolean formulas with `k`
2054:  alternating blocks, is complete for the `k`-th level of the hierarchy
2055:  ([Stockmeyer 1976][stockmeyer1976polynomial]; [Wrathall
2056:  1976][wrathall1976complete]) by the same Tseitin discharge carrying block
2057:  marks.
2058:* **At PSPACE**: SUCCINCT-REACH (`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.SuccinctReach`)
2059:  – reachability in a transition system whose states are the truth assignments
2060:  to marked *state variables* and whose transitions, sources and targets are
2061:  described by three CNF formulas rather than listed – is PSPACE-complete
2062:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.SUCCINCTREACH_PSPACE_complete`). The two halves are the
2063:  two readings of one identification, and they mirror the Cook–Levin pair
2064:  exactly. Membership is cheap for the structural reason that makes every
2065:  reachability logic's image cheap: the problem *is* the syntactic image of
2066:  SO(TC), so the specification is a transcription. Its four monadic relation
2067:  variables are the state being walked plus the three existential witnesses –
2068:  one per clause group – that a transitive closure cannot quantify on its own;
2069:  two endpoint witnesses rather than one, because a walk of length zero must
2070:  meet both endpoint conditions at the same state. Hardness Tseitin-encodes the
2071:  three sentences of a `DescriptiveComplexity.SOTCSpec` into the three clause
2072:  groups, reusing the semantic core of the SAT discharge unchanged
2073:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.Tseitin.satCond_iff_gates`); what is new is that the three
2074:  encodings are taken over the *doubled* block
2075:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.SOBlock.double`), so that the propositional variables for
2076:  the atoms of the block are the same elements in all three – they are exactly
2077:  the state variables, their second copies the next-state copies. A state of
2078:  the interpreted system is therefore an assignment of the block and nothing
2079:  else, and the two walks correspond step by step, with no initialization or
2080:  finalization steps to peel off.
2081:* **At PSPACE, again**: QSAT (`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Qsat`) – is a fully
2082:  quantified Boolean formula true, when the quantifier prefix is *part of the
2083:  instance* rather than fixed by the problem? – is PSPACE-complete
2084:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.QSAT_PSPACE_complete`; [Stockmeyer–Meyer
2085:  1973][stockmeyer1973word]). That an instance carries its own prefix is exactly
2086:  the step from the polynomial hierarchy to PSPACE, and it is what the semantics
2087:  has to pay for: a position is a set of already-quantified variables together
2088:  with a valuation, the next variable to play is the least unplayed one, and the
2089:  game value is an inductive predicate rather than a recursion, so that it is
2090:  defined on infinite structures too. Membership walks that game tree
2091:  depth-first, short-circuiting so that no accumulator is needed – four relation
2092:  variables and four transitions. Hardness is Savitch's recursive doubling
2093:  ([Savitch 1970][savitch1970relationships]) written as an interpretation:
2094:  reachability in at most `2 ^ m` steps, `m` the number of state variables of a
2095:  SUCCINCT-REACH instance, unfolds into a prefix of `m` blocks `∃Z_ℓ ∀b_ℓ
2096:  ∃(U_ℓ, V_ℓ)`, the universal bit choosing which half of the level is checked and
2097:  a *fresh copy* of the pair receiving it – which is what keeps the matrix
2098:  clausal, so that no Tseitin encoding is needed anywhere. Two things make the
2099:  proof go through: the vertices of the walk are states only up to their
2100:  restriction to the state variables, which is why `DescriptiveComplexity.Savitch`
2101:  is stated for a relation classified into a finite type; and the prefix is a
2102:  lexicographic comparison of static keys, so that its blocks are the sets of
2103:  variables sharing the first three components of a key and the peeling lemmas of
2104:  `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Qsat.Blocks` apply level by level.
2105:* **Between NP and the second level**: SAT-UNSAT – is the first of two CNF
2106:  formulas satisfiable and the second not? – is DP-complete
2107:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.SATUNSAT_DP_complete`; [Papadimitriou & Yannakakis
2108:  1984][papadimitriou1984complexity]). Membership is the shape of the problem
2109:  itself; hardness runs *two* Cook–Levin discharges, one for the `Σ₁` half and
2110:  one for the complement of the `Π₁` half, side by side into a single paired
2111:  instance. Pairing forces a common universe, so each side's tuples are pinned
2112:  to canonically padded ones: with the spare coordinates left free, every clause
2113:  and variable would acquire copies and an unsatisfiable formula could blow up
2114:  into a satisfiable one.
2115:
2116:* **Complete, but not for a class**: Digraph Isomorphism
2117:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.DigraphIso`) – are the two marked directed
2118:  graphs of the instance isomorphic? – is in NP by a textbook `Σ₁` guessing the bijection
2119:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.digraphIso_mem_NP`), with no order, no counting and no
2120:  threshold, and is the library's first problem conjecturally neither in P nor
2121:  NP-complete ([Babai 2016][babai2016graph]; [Köbler, Schöning and Torán
2122:  1993][kobler1993graph]). What it *is* complete for is its own degree
2123:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.digraphIso_GI_complete`), which is the whole point of
2124:  `DescriptiveComplexity.ComplexityClass.below`, and that degree lies inside NP
2125:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.GI_subset_NP`). It is also the problem of deciding the
2126:  very equivalence a `DescriptiveComplexity.DecisionProblem` is required to be
2127:  invariant under: `DescriptiveComplexity.relIsoOn_iff_equiv` states the
2128:  semantics as the existence of an equivalence between the two marked sets
2129:  carrying one adjacency relation to the other. **DAG Isomorphism**
2130:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.DagIso`) is the first companion in that
2131:  degree, GI-complete (`DescriptiveComplexity.dagIso_GI_complete`): hardness
2132:  subdivides every arc *twice*, so that its direction survives as the
2133:  difference between the two subdivision levels, and membership forgets the
2134:  topological order the instances carry. They carry one because acyclicity is
2135:  not first-order definable, so a reduction could not otherwise test it – the
2136:  place where the first-order setting genuinely constrains what a problem may
2137:  be, and where a polynomial-time reduction would simply run a cycle check.
2138:  **Graph Isomorphism** proper – the simple-graph problem the literature names
2139:  GI (`DescriptiveComplexity.GraphIso`) – is **GI-complete**
2140:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.graphIso_GI_complete`): simplicity is first-order, so
2141:  one direction only tests it, and the other is the classical digraph-to-graph
2142:  gadget – every arc subdivided three times, each vertex carrying a lollipop
2143:  and each tail a pendant, so that the levels are recovered from adjacency
2144:  alone and the pendant carries the arc's direction. The degree is *defined* on
2145:  this problem – the literature's GI is the undirected one – and the directed
2146:  problem is complete for it too
2147:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.digraphIso_GI_complete`,
2148:  `DescriptiveComplexity.GI_eq_below_digraphIso`). The shared layer for
2149:  reductions between isomorphism problems is `DescriptiveComplexity.IsoGadget`:
2150:  it reads a marked binary relation as a
2151:  `FirstOrder.Language.graph`-structure in its own right, so that the semantic
2152:  condition of every problem in the degree becomes an isomorphism of the two
2153:  sides (`DescriptiveComplexity.relIsoOn_iff_nonempty_sideEquiv`) and a gadget's
2154:  correctness can be stated on *single* graphs instead of twice over, once per
2155:  side. `DescriptiveComplexity.TwoCopies` is the other half of that layer: the
2156:  vocabulary `FirstOrder.Language.twoCopies L₁` – two marks and two copies of
2157:  every symbol of `L₁` – together with the problem
2158:  `DescriptiveComplexity.TwoCopiesIso` asking whether the two marked
2159:  `L₁`-structures of an instance are isomorphic. A gadget can be *doubled* – run
2160:  relativized to each mark – only against a target of that shape, the defining
2161:  formulas having to be given symbol by symbol; problems joining the degree from
2162:  here on are meant to be stated over it.
2163:  `DescriptiveComplexity.GadgetDouble` closes the layer: it doubles a gadget –
2164:  a construction on *single* structures – by renaming its atoms to each side's
2165:  copy and relativizing its quantifiers to that side's mark, and identifies the
2166:  sides of the result (`DescriptiveComplexity.patSideDoubleEquiv`: the pattern
2167:  side of the doubled gadget is the gadget on the pattern side). What a client
2168:  then owes is `DescriptiveComplexity.IsoReflecting`, “isomorphic values come
2169:  from isomorphic arguments”, a statement about single structures with no
2170:  pattern/host distinction in it; the converse is free by functoriality, and
2171:  `DescriptiveComplexity.isoReflecting_fo_reduction` turns the pair into an
2172:  order-free reduction.
2173:
2174:* **At RE**: FINSAT (`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.FinSat`) – does a
2175:  first-order sentence, encoded as a finite structure, have a *finite* model? –
2176:  is RE-complete (`DescriptiveComplexity.FINSAT_RE_complete`), which is
2177:  Trakhtenbrot's theorem in the logical form. FINSAT is the syntactic image of
2178:  `∃SO[new]` exactly as SAT is that of `Σ₁`: a certificate is “a finite
2179:  extension of the universe plus relations on it satisfying a fixed first-order
2180:  kernel”, a finite model is “a finite universe plus relations on it satisfying
2181:  a given first-order sentence”, and the reduction translates the first into the
2182:  second. Two decisions carry the encoding: the instance is a parse DAG **in
2183:  negation normal form**, so that the value of a node is monotone in its
2184:  children and satisfaction is a least fixed point rather than a well-founded
2185:  recursion on a decoded parse tree – there is no decoding, the symbols of the
2186:  encoded sentence being elements of the instance – and its ∧/∨ nodes are
2187:  **n-ary**, so that the unbounded conjunctions of the reduction are single
2188:  nodes. The encoded sentence carries its own quantifiers, so the reduction
2189:  needs no context tuples, and its vocabulary is *only* the relation variables of
2190:  the block: `old` and the symbols of the source are translated away into
2191:  disjunctions indexed by the tuples the interpretation's own formulas select.
2192:  The source vocabulary is relational, as every vocabulary of a
2193:  `DescriptiveComplexity.DecisionProblem` is.
2194:
2195:  The **halting problem** (`DescriptiveComplexity.HALT`) is the same machine data
2196:  as the NP and PSPACE bridges with *both* bounds dropped: the tape is an
2197:  unbounded strip of pages, each a copy of the instance's positions, so no
2198:  arithmetic enters the model and the input needs no placement. It is in RE
2199:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.halt_mem_RE`) because a run – finite, but bounded by no
2200:  function of the instance – is exactly what value invention guesses; and since
2201:  FINSAT is already RE-hard, that yields
2202:  `DescriptiveComplexity.halt_le_finsat` at once: the halting problem
2203:  first-order-reduces to finite satisfiability, which is Trakhtenbrot's theorem in
2204:  the form it is usually stated. RE-*hardness* of `HALT`
2205:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.halt_RE_hard`, whence
2206:  `DescriptiveComplexity.halt_RE_complete`) is the machine bridge: the
2207:  reduction draws a **fixed** simulating machine – its states, symbols and
2208:  transitions are tags, free at every instance size – and spells the
2209:  instance's own relation tables as a chain of one-bit `comp` frames on the
2210:  initial tape, folded at run time into the one number that a semi-decision
2211:  code – named by `Turing.ToPartrec.Code.exists_code`, never built – decodes
2212:  back into the instance. The simulation of the code model on one unbounded
2213:  tape is a string-rewriting argument against the same configuration-word
2214:  layer the PCP reduction uses, so the tape-function bookkeeping is paid for
2215:  once (`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Machine.HaltHard`).
2216:
2217:  **Post's correspondence problem** (`DescriptiveComplexity.PCP`,
2218:  [Post 1946][post1946variant]) has the same membership half
2219:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.pcp_mem_RE`, whence
2220:  `DescriptiveComplexity.pcp_le_finsat`): a match is a nonempty sequence of
2221:  marked dominoes whose top words and bottom words have the same concatenation,
2222:  the words of a domino being its letters read in the order the instance
2223:  carries on their positions. It is the first catalog problem whose certificate
2224:  is a *sequence* rather than a structure, and the common word it spells is
2225:  **never invented**: its letters are indexed by the pairs (slot, position of
2226:  the word sitting there) in lexicographic order, once for each of the two
2227:  parses, and what the certificate carries is a **matching** between the two
2228:  index lists. A first-order kernel can ask of a relation variable only that it
2229:  land in the two parses, be defined everywhere on both, reflect the two orders
2230:  and preserve letters, and that is already enough
2231:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.Pcp.forall₂_of_matching`): such a relation pairs the
2232:  entries of two strictly sorted lists index by index, so the two
2233:  concatenations agree letter by letter.
2234:
2235:  Being a sequence is also why `PCP` is not a second syntactic image:
2236:  RE-*hardness* is the classical computation-history construction
2237:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.halt_ordered_fo_reduction_pcp`). A `HALT` instance
2238:  carries its transitions as elements, so the interpretation emits one
2239:  decorated domino per transition-attribute tuple – the words are data, read
2240:  off one shared table – plus a start domino spelling the initial
2241:  configuration, and a match is exactly a halting derivation of the machine's
2242:  rewriting system. With `HALT` RE-hard this makes PCP **RE-complete**
2243:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.pcp_RE_complete`) and Post's problem undecidable
2244:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.pcp_not_computable`).
2245:
2246:  **CODEHALT** (`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.CodeHalt`) – does the
2247:  `Nat.Partrec.Code` drawn as the syntax tree of the instance halt on `0`? – is
2248:  **RE-complete** (`DescriptiveComplexity.codehalt_RE_complete`), and its
2249:  hardness proof is general enough to give the identity of the class with its
2250:  machine reading: `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_RE_iff_rePred`, a problem is in
2251:  RE exactly when its concrete instances are semi-decidable. The reduction
2252:  writes the instance *as a program*: the root of the drawn code is
2253:  `comp cP (pair numeral nest)`, where `cP` is a code semi-deciding the source
2254:  problem – supplied by `Nat.Partrec.Code.exists_code`, never built – and the
2255:  rest is a constant that first-order formulas can draw. Since every branch is
2256:  evaluated at input `0`, a constant is a tree of `pair`, `succ` and `zero`
2257:  nodes, so a bit of the input instance is *one node*, and the table is nested
2258:  by coordinate rather than numbered in a mixed radix: each level of the nest
2259:  is then a plain walk of the input order, which is what a first-order guard
2260:  can describe, and no arithmetic on positions appears anywhere. The two
2261:  shared leaves `succ` and `zero` let a bit be read as an *edge* of the
2262:  drawing rather than as a mark, so every element has exactly one constructor
2263:  and the drawing is well formed by inspection. Three headlines come out of
2264:  the one construction: RE-completeness of `CODEHALT`, `RE = REPred`, and –
2265:  with Post's theorem and the undecidability of `CODEHALT` –
2266:  `DescriptiveComplexity.RE_ne_coRE`.

73:/-- A decision problem in the sense of descriptive complexity: an
74:isomorphism-closed property of `L`-structures, whose yes-instances are the
75:`L`-structures satisfying it. Isomorphism-invariance is part of the notion –
76:a decision problem cannot distinguish isomorphic presentations of the same
77:structure.
78:
79:The vocabulary is *relational*, as everywhere in finite model theory: the
80:instance argument makes the convention structural, so every notion built on
81:decision problems – interpretations, reductions, complexity classes –
82:inherits it once and for all. -/
83:structure DecisionProblem [L.IsRelational] where
84:  /-- The predicate: `P A` (through the function coercion) states that the
85:  structure `A` is a yes-instance. -/
86:  Holds : ∀ (A : Type) [L.Structure A], Prop
87:  /-- Decision problems do not distinguish isomorphic structures. -/
88:  iso_invariant : ∀ {A B : Type} [L.Structure A] [L.Structure B],
89:    (A ≃[L] B) → (Holds A ↔ Holds B)
90:
91:namespace DecisionProblem
92:
93:variable {L} [L.IsRelational]
94:
95:instance : CoeFun (DecisionProblem L) fun _ => ∀ (A : Type) [L.Structure A], Prop :=
96:  ⟨Holds⟩
97:
98:@[ext]
99:theorem ext {P Q : DecisionProblem L} (h : ∀ (A : Type) [L.Structure A], P A ↔ Q A) :
100:    P = Q := by
101:  obtain ⟨p, hp⟩ := P
102:  obtain ⟨q, hq⟩ := Q
103:  have : p = q := funext fun A => funext fun inst => propext (h A)
104:  subst this
105:  rfl
106:
107:end DecisionProblem
