109:/-! ### Transport of relations along isomorphisms
110:
111:Proving the `iso_invariant` field of a `DecisionProblem` always starts the
112:same way: the semantic property is phrased in terms of `RelMap r ![a]` /
113:`RelMap r ![a, b]`, and one must know that these transport along an
114:`L`-isomorphism. The two lemmas below package this step once and for all
115:(`Mathlib`'s `StrongHomClass.map_rel` states it with `e ∘ ![a, b]`, which
116:must first be normalized to `![e a, e b]`). -/
117:
118:section RelMapTransport
119:
120:variable {L} {A B : Type} [L.Structure A] [L.Structure B]
121:
122:/-- A unary relation transports along an `L`-isomorphism. -/
123:theorem relMap_equiv₁ (e : A ≃[L] B) (r : L.Relations 1) (a : A) :
124:    RelMap r ![a] ↔ RelMap r ![e a] := by
125:  have h := StrongHomClass.map_rel e r ![a]
126:  have hv : e ∘ ![a] = ![e a] := by
127:    funext j
128:    fin_cases j
129:    simp
130:  rw [hv] at h
131:  exact h.symm
132:
133:/-- A binary relation transports along an `L`-isomorphism. -/
134:theorem relMap_equiv₂ (e : A ≃[L] B) (r : L.Relations 2) (a b : A) :
135:    RelMap r ![a, b] ↔ RelMap r ![e a, e b] := by
136:  have h := StrongHomClass.map_rel e r ![a, b]
137:  have hv : e ∘ ![a, b] = ![e a, e b] := by
138:    funext j
139:    fin_cases j <;> simp
140:  rw [hv] at h
141:  exact h.symm
142:
143:/-- A ternary relation transports along an `L`-isomorphism. -/
144:theorem relMap_equiv₃ (e : A ≃[L] B) (r : L.Relations 3) (a b c : A) :
145:    RelMap r ![a, b, c] ↔ RelMap r ![e a, e b, e c] := by
146:  have h := StrongHomClass.map_rel e r ![a, b, c]
147:  have hv : e ∘ ![a, b, c] = ![e a, e b, e c] := by
148:    funext j
149:    fin_cases j <;> simp
150:  rw [hv] at h
151:  exact h.symm

153:/-- Realization of an atom of arity 3, the shape Mathlib's
154:`Formula.realize_rel₁` and `Formula.realize_rel₂` stop short of. -/
155:theorem realize_rel₃ {L : Language} {α M : Type} [L.Structure M] {R : L.Relations 3}
156:    {t₁ t₂ t₃ : L.Term α} {v : α → M} :
157:    (R.formula ![t₁, t₂, t₃]).Realize v ↔
158:      RelMap R ![t₁.realize v, t₂.realize v, t₃.realize v] := by
159:  rw [Formula.realize_rel, iff_eq_eq]
160:  congr 1
161:  funext i
162:  fin_cases i <;> rfl

176:/-- A *tagged `dim`-dimensional first-order interpretation* of the relational
177:language `L'` in the language `L`. It maps an `L`-structure `A` to the
178:`L'`-structure with universe `Tag × A^dim` in which an `n`-ary relation symbol
179:`R` holds of tagged tuples `(t₁, ā₁), …, (tₙ, āₙ)` iff the first-order
180:`L`-formula `relFormula R (t₁, …, tₙ)` – whose free variable `(i, j)` stands
181:for the `j`-th coordinate `āᵢ j` of the `i`-th argument – holds in `A`. -/
182:structure FOInterpretation (Tag : Type) (dim : ℕ) where
183:  /-- The defining `L`-formula of each relation symbol of `L'`, for each tuple
184:  of tags; the free variable `(i, j)` is the `j`-th coordinate of the `i`-th
185:  argument tuple. -/
186:  relFormula : ∀ {n : ℕ}, L'.Relations n → (Fin n → Tag) → L.Formula (Fin n × Fin dim)
187:
188:namespace FOInterpretation
189:
190:variable {L L' : Language.{0, 0}} {Tag : Type} {dim : ℕ}
191:
192:/-- The universe of the structure interpreted in `A`: tagged `dim`-tuples.
193:
194:This is a plain `def` (not an `abbrev`) so that the `L'.Structure` instance on
195:it can be found by instance search, while `rcases`-style destructuring still
196:sees through it. -/
197:protected def Map (_I : FOInterpretation L L' Tag dim) (A : Type) : Type :=
198:  Tag × (Fin dim → A)
199:
200:variable (I : FOInterpretation L L' Tag dim) (A : Type) [L.Structure A]
201:
202:/-- The `L'`-structure interpreted in the `L`-structure `A`. -/

232:/-- A first-order reduction from the problem `P` (on `L`-structures) to the
233:problem `Q` (on `L'`-structures): a first-order interpretation mapping
234:yes-instances of `P` exactly to yes-instances of `Q`.
235:
236:Since FO interpretations are computable in AC⁰ ⊆ PTIME on (encodings of)
237:finite structures, an `FOReduction P Q` is in particular a Karp reduction from
238:`P` to `Q`: any NP-hardness argument for `P` transfers to `Q`, without any
239:formalized machine model. -/
240:structure FOReduction [L.IsRelational] [L'.IsRelational] (P : DecisionProblem L)
241:    (Q : DecisionProblem L') where
242:  /-- The tags (copies of `A^dim`) used by the underlying interpretation. -/
243:  Tag : Type
244:  /-- Tags are finite, so that finite structures map to finite structures. -/
245:  [tagFinite : Finite Tag]
246:  /-- Tags are nonempty, so that nonempty structures map to nonempty
247:  structures. -/
248:  [tagNonempty : Nonempty Tag]
249:  /-- The dimension of the underlying interpretation. -/
250:  dim : ℕ
251:  /-- The underlying first-order interpretation. -/
252:  toInterpretation : FOInterpretation L L' Tag dim
253:  /-- Yes-instances map exactly to yes-instances, on the *finite* nonempty
254:  structures: membership and hardness read a problem only there
255:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.ComplexityClass`), so asking anything of the infinite
256:  ones would be an obligation nothing consumes. The ordered and relativized
257:  notions restrict the same way. -/
258:  correct : ∀ (A : Type) [L.Structure A] [Finite A] [Nonempty A],
259:    P A ↔ Q (toInterpretation.Map A)
260:

262:scoped notation:50 P:51 " ≤ᶠᵒ " Q:51 => FOReduction P Q

45:(ordered) first-order reductions. Both predicates are left completely
46:abstract; the closure requirements are sound for every class containing
47:LOGSPACE, since (ordered) FO reductions are computable in AC⁰.
48:
49:Hardness is a field of its own rather than a function of `Mem`: the naive
50:“every member reduces to `P`” cannot even be stated here, since a reduction
51:has a *relational* target while `Hard` ranges over arbitrary vocabularies. The
52:classes of this library take it to be cofinal hardness for their own members
53:and are built by `DescriptiveComplexity.ComplexityClass.ofMem`, which supplies both
54:that reading of `Hard` and the three closure proofs it needs; keeping the field
55:abstract leaves room for the two that read hardness differently
56:(`DescriptiveComplexity.ComplexityClass.empty`, `DescriptiveComplexity.PH`). -/
57:structure ComplexityClass where
58:  /-- The problems belonging to the class. Use the notation `P ∈ 𝒞`. -/
59:  Mem : ∀ {L : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational], DecisionProblem L → Prop
60:  /-- The problems every problem of the class reduces to (“`𝒞`-hard”). -/
61:  Hard : ∀ {L : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational], DecisionProblem L → Prop
62:  /-- Membership travels backward along FO reductions. -/
63:  mem_of_foReduction : ∀ {L L' : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] [L'.IsRelational]
64:    {P : DecisionProblem L} {Q : DecisionProblem L'}, (P ≤ᶠᵒ Q) → Mem Q → Mem P
65:  /-- Hardness travels forward along FO reductions. -/
66:  hard_of_foReduction : ∀ {L L' : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] [L'.IsRelational]
67:    {P : DecisionProblem L} {Q : DecisionProblem L'}, (P ≤ᶠᵒ Q) → Hard P → Hard Q
68:  /-- Membership travels backward along ordered FO reductions. -/
69:  mem_of_orderedReduction : ∀ {L L' : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] [L'.IsRelational]
70:    {P : DecisionProblem L} {Q : DecisionProblem L'}, (P ≤ᶠᵒ[≤] Q) → Mem Q → Mem P
71:  /-- Hardness travels forward along ordered FO reductions. -/
72:  hard_of_orderedReduction : ∀ {L L' : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] [L'.IsRelational]
73:    {P : DecisionProblem L} {Q : DecisionProblem L'}, (P ≤ᶠᵒ[≤] Q) → Hard P → Hard Q
74:  /-- Hardness travels forward along relativized ordered FO reductions – the
75:  reductions with a definable target universe, needed for spanning problems. -/
76:  hard_of_relOrderedReduction : ∀ {L L' : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] [L'.IsRelational]
77:    {P : DecisionProblem L} {Q : DecisionProblem L'}, (P ≤ʳᶠᵒ[≤] Q) → Hard P → Hard Q
78:  /-- Complexity classes speak about *finite* instances only: membership does
79:  not depend on the behavior of a problem on infinite structures. -/
80:  mem_congr_finite : ∀ {L : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] {P Q : DecisionProblem L},
81:    (∀ (A : Type) [L.Structure A] [Finite A], P A ↔ Q A) → (Mem P ↔ Mem Q)
82:  /-- Hardness, too, only depends on the finite instances of a problem. -/
83:  hard_congr_finite : ∀ {L : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] {P Q : DecisionProblem L},
84:    (∀ (A : Type) [L.Structure A] [Finite A], P A ↔ Q A) → (Hard P ↔ Hard Q)
85:

87:overloads the `∈` notation; the `Membership` class cannot be used here since
88:the element type `DecisionProblem L` is not determined by `ComplexityClass`.) -/
89:scoped notation:50 P:51 " ∈ " C:51 => ComplexityClass.Mem C P

93:/-- Two complexity classes with the same members and the same hard problems
94:are equal: the remaining fields are proofs. -/
95:theorem ext {C₁ C₂ : ComplexityClass}
96:    (hMem : ∀ {L : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] (P : DecisionProblem L),
97:      C₁.Mem P ↔ C₂.Mem P)
98:    (hHard : ∀ {L : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] (P : DecisionProblem L),
99:      C₁.Hard P ↔ C₂.Hard P) :
100:    C₁ = C₂ := by
101:  obtain ⟨M₁, H₁, _, _, _, _, _, _, _⟩ := C₁
102:  obtain ⟨M₂, H₂, _, _, _, _, _, _, _⟩ := C₂
103:  have hM : @M₁ = @M₂ := by
104:    funext L inst P
105:    exact propext (hMem P)
106:  have hH : @H₁ = @H₂ := by
107:    funext L inst P
108:    exact propext (hHard P)
109:  subst hM
110:  subst hH
111:  rfl

113:/-- The empty complexity class: no members, and every problem vacuously hard
114:(there is nothing that would have to reduce to it). It stands for a level of a
115:hierarchy that has no logical characterization. -/
116:def empty : ComplexityClass where
117:  Mem _ := False
118:  Hard _ := True
119:  mem_of_foReduction _ h := h
120:  hard_of_foReduction _ _ := trivial
121:  mem_of_orderedReduction _ h := h
122:  hard_of_orderedReduction _ _ := trivial
123:  hard_of_relOrderedReduction _ _ := trivial
124:  mem_congr_finite _ := Iff.rfl
125:  hard_congr_finite _ := Iff.rfl

247:/-! ### Polynomial time, by the Horn fragment -/
248:
249:/-- **The class PTIME**: the problems definable in the Horn fragment SO-Horn of
250:existential second-order logic ([Grädel 1992][gradel1992capturing]), which
251:captures polynomial time on ordered structures. It is a bona fide
252:`DescriptiveComplexity.ComplexityClass` because SO-Horn definability is closed under
253:(ordered) first-order reductions – the Horn shape survives the pullback, see
254:`DescriptiveComplexity.SecondOrderHornPull`.
255:
256:This is level 0 of the hierarchy below (`DescriptiveComplexity.SigmaP`,
257:`DescriptiveComplexity.PiP`), and it has a complete problem, HORN-SAT
258:(`DescriptiveComplexity.HORNSAT_PTIME_complete`). That the class is closed under
259:complement – `PiP 0 = SigmaP 0` – is `DescriptiveComplexity.piP_zero_eq`, through the
260:equivalence with FO(LFP). -/
261:noncomputable def PTIME : ComplexityClass :=
262:  .ofMem (fun P => SigmaSOHornDefinable P)
263:    (fun f h => h.of_foReduction f)

267:/-! ### The hierarchy -/
268:
269:/-- The `Σₖᵖ` levels of the polynomial hierarchy: polynomial time at level 0
270:(`DescriptiveComplexity.PTIME`, defined by the Horn fragment SO-Horn), second-order
271:definability with `k` alternations above. -/
272:noncomputable def SigmaP : ℕ → ComplexityClass
273:  | 0 => PTIME
274:  | k + 1 => sigmaLevel k
275:
276:/-- The `Πₖᵖ` levels of the polynomial hierarchy; level 0 is *co*-polynomial
277:time, the complements of the SO-Horn definable problems. That this coincides
278:with `DescriptiveComplexity.PTIME` is the closure of polynomial time under complement,
279:`DescriptiveComplexity.piP_zero_eq` – see the module docstring. -/
280:noncomputable def PiP : ℕ → ComplexityClass
281:  | 0 => PTIME.compl
282:  | k + 1 => piLevel k
283:
284:/-- NP is `Σ₁ᵖ`: by definition, the existential-second-order definable
285:problems (Fagin's theorem). -/
286:noncomputable abbrev NP : ComplexityClass := SigmaP 1
287:
288:/-- coNP is `Π₁ᵖ`: the universal-second-order definable problems. -/
289:noncomputable abbrev coNP : ComplexityClass := PiP 1
290:
291:/-- **`Πₖᵖ` consists of the complements of the `Σₖᵖ` problems**, at every
292:level: by definition at level 0, and by the quantifier duality
293:`DescriptiveComplexity.piSODefinable_iff_compl` above from level 1 on.
294:
295:(That moreover `PiP 0 = SigmaP 0` – polynomial time closed under complement –
296:is `DescriptiveComplexity.piP_zero_eq`: complementing a Horn program needs its least
297:model computed inside the fragment, which is what the translation from FO(LFP)
298:provides.) -/
299:theorem mem_piP_iff (k : ℕ) {L : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] (P : DecisionProblem L) :
300:    P ∈ PiP k ↔ Pᶜ ∈ SigmaP k := by
301:  cases k with
302:  | zero => exact Iff.rfl
303:  | succ k => exact piSODefinable_iff_compl (k + 1) P
304:

13:/-!
14:# The logically defined classes are the degrees of their complete problems
15:
16:Each class of this library with a complete problem `Q₀` *is* the degree of `Q₀`
17:(`DescriptiveComplexity.ComplexityClass.below`, the file
18:`DescriptiveComplexity.Degree`): `NP = below SAT`, `coNP = below TAUT`,
19:`PTIME = below HORNSAT`, `NL = below TwoSAT` and `RE = below FINSAT`. This is
20:the sanity check that the degree construction is the right one – and a theorem
21:rather than a tautology, since the two sides are defined completely
22:differently: on the left a logic, on the right a closure under reductions.
23:
24:The payoff is that “`Q₀`-hardness is `𝒞`-hardness” stops being folklore: since
25:the classes are *equal*, so are their hardness predicates, whichever way a
26:given hardness proof was obtained.
27:
28:Each proof supplies `DescriptiveComplexity.ComplexityClass.eq_below_of_complete`
29:with the class's own hardness discharge, which delivers the *non-relativized*
30:reduction `≤ᶠᵒ[≤]` that the equality needs – cofinal hardness on its own yields
31:only `≤ʳᶠᵒ[≤]`. This is why the statement cannot be proved generically, for an
32:arbitrary class and an arbitrary complete problem of it.
33:-/

10:# The Cook–Levin theorem: hardness of SAT
11:
12:The hardness half of the Cook–Levin theorem ([Cook 1971][cook1971complexity];
13:[Levin 1973][levin1973universal]), machine-free and in the style of Dahlhaus
14:([Dahlhaus 1983][dahlhaus1983reduction]): every existential-second-order
15:definable problem admits an ordered
16:first-order reduction to SAT
17:(`DescriptiveComplexity.sat_hard_of_sigmaSODefinable`). Since NP is *defined* as
18:`Σ₁`-definability (`DescriptiveComplexity.Hierarchy`), together with the membership
19:half `DescriptiveComplexity.sat_sigmaSODefinable` this makes SAT NP-complete
20:(`DescriptiveComplexity.SAT_NP_complete`) – relying on no axioms beyond
21:Lean's standard three, as `#print axioms` confirms.
22:
23:Given the single second-order block `B` and the first-order kernel `φ` of a
24:`Σ₁` definition of a problem `Q`, the reduction interprets, inside an ordered
25:input structure `A`, the CNF instance of the Tseitin encoding
26:([Tseitin 1968][tseitin1968complexity]) of `φ`
27:(`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Sat.Tseitin`):
28:
29:* propositional variables: one per relation variable `i` of `B` and
30:  `B.arity i`-tuple over `A` (element `(Sum.inr (Sum.inl i), x)`), and one
FILE DescriptiveComplexity/Problems/Sat/Hardness.lean 325-370
325:      Q A ↔ SORealize L A [B] φ true) : Q ≤ᶠᵒ[≤] SAT where
326:  Tag := TseitinTag B φ
327:  dim := tseitinDim B φ
328:  toInterpretation := tseitinInterp B φ
329:  correct A _ _ _ _ :=
330:    (hφ A).trans ((sorealize_head_iff B φ).trans
331:      (tseitin_satisfiable_iff B φ A).symm)

335:/-! ### The Cook–Levin theorem -/
336:
337:/-- The hardness half of the Cook–Levin theorem: every
338:existential-second-order definable problem admits an ordered first-order
339:reduction to SAT. Machine-free NP-hardness in the style of Dahlhaus, by the
340:generic Tseitin reduction `DescriptiveComplexity.tseitinReduction`. -/
341:theorem sat_hard_of_sigmaSODefinable :
342:    ∀ {L : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] (Q : DecisionProblem L),
343:      SigmaSODefinable 1 Q → Nonempty (Q ≤ᶠᵒ[≤] SAT) := by
344:  rintro L _ Q ⟨Bs, hlen, φ, hφ⟩
345:  cases Bs with
346:  | nil => exact absurd hlen (by simp)
347:  | cons B Bs' =>
348:    cases Bs' with
349:    | nil => exact ⟨tseitinReduction B φ Q hφ⟩
350:    | cons B' Bs'' => simp at hlen

353:`DescriptiveComplexity.sat_sigmaSODefinable`; hardness is
354:`DescriptiveComplexity.sat_hard_of_sigmaSODefinable`, the generic Tseitin reduction. -/
355:theorem SAT_NP_complete : NP.Complete SAT :=
356:  ⟨sat_sigmaSODefinable,
357:    (hard_sigmaP_succ_iff 0 SAT).mpr fun Q hQ =>

14:/-!
15:# HORN-SAT
16:
17:Umbrella file for HORN-SAT, propositional satisfiability restricted to
18:formulas with at most one positive literal per clause: the canonical complete
19:problem for polynomial time.
20:
21:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.HornSat.Defs`: the problem
22:  `DescriptiveComplexity.HORNSAT`, over the SAT vocabulary with the Horn condition
23:  `DescriptiveComplexity.AtMostOnePositive` folded into the yes-instances;
24:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.HornSat.Membership`: `HORNSAT ∈ NP`, the SAT kernel
25:  conjoined with the first-order Horn condition;
26:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.HornSat.Hardness`: the *Horn discharge* – every
27:  SO-Horn definable problem (`DescriptiveComplexity.SigmaSOHornDefinable`) admits an
28:  ordered first-order reduction to HORN-SAT;
29:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.HornSat.Unsat`: `HORNSAT ∈ coNP`, by a first-order
30:  checkable certificate of Horn *un*satisfiability (a derivation-closed set
31:  with its derivation order). HORN-SAT is thus in `NP ∩ coNP`, as a
32:  polynomial-time problem should be, and complementing the discharge gives the
33:  level-0 inclusions of the hierarchy;
34:* `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.HornSat.Definability`: `HORNSAT ∈ PTIME`, the Horn
35:  program computing unit propagation – which with the discharge makes HORN-SAT
36:  **PTIME-complete**.
37:
38:What the two halves add up to is stated at the end of this file:
39:`DescriptiveComplexity.hornSat_PTIME_hard` and `DescriptiveComplexity.PTIME_subset_NP`.
40:
41:## What the hardness statement says, and what it does not
42:
43:The discharge `DescriptiveComplexity.hornSat_hard_of_sigmaSOHornDefinable` is the exact
44:analogue, one level down, of the Cook–Levin discharge
45:`DescriptiveComplexity.sat_hard_of_sigmaSODefinable`: it is the reason SAT is NP-hard
46:transposed to the Horn fragment, and it is meaningful *before* polynomial time
47:is defined – it says that HORN-SAT is at least as hard as everything the Horn
48:fragment can express. It is also markedly simpler, since a Horn program needs
49:no Tseitin gates.
50:
51:One thing is deliberately *not* claimed: **Grädel's capture theorem against
52:machines is not formalized.** That SO-Horn captures polynomial time on ordered
53:structures ([Grädel 1992][gradel1992capturing]) has a direction – every
54:machine-polynomial-time problem is SO-Horn definable – that simulates a
55:machine, and so lies outside a machine-model-free library. So
56:`DescriptiveComplexity.PTIME` is *defined* as SO-Horn definability, exactly as NP is
57:defined as `Σ₁`-definability, and the identification with the
58:machine-theoretic class stays a citation.
59:
60:Closure of level 0 under complement, by contrast, *is* a theorem. Since
61:HORN-SAT is PTIME-complete, `PiP 0 = SigmaP 0` is equivalent to a single crisp
62:question: **is Horn *un*satisfiability SO-Horn definable?** The certificate of
63:`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.HornSat.Unsat` only puts it in NP, and the fragment
64:cannot do it head-on: a Horn program accepts when the least model of its rules
65:satisfies its goal clauses, so to accept the *unsatisfiable* instances one
66:would have to derive a contradiction from a universally quantified statement
67:about the least model – the negative information a goal clause cannot supply.
68:The route that works is the logic-to-logic equivalence SO-Horn = FO(LFP) of
69:`DescriptiveComplexity.FixedPointHorn`, a full logic being closed under negation by
70:construction; `DescriptiveComplexity.hornSat_compl_mem_PTIME` below is the resulting
71:answer, and `DescriptiveComplexity.piP_zero_eq` the resulting identity.
72:-/
73:
74:namespace DescriptiveComplexity
75:
76:/-- **HORN-SAT is PTIME-hard**, machine-free: every SO-Horn definable problem
77:admits an ordered first-order reduction to it. -/
78:theorem hornSat_PTIME_hard : PTIME.Hard HORNSAT :=
79:  (hard_PTIME_iff HORNSAT).mpr fun Q hQ =>
80:    (hornSat_hard_of_sigmaSOHornDefinable Q hQ).map OrderedFOReduction.toRel
81:
82:/-- **HORN-SAT is PTIME-complete.** Membership is
83:`DescriptiveComplexity.hornSat_mem_PTIME` – the Horn program that computes unit
84:propagation, assembling the unbounded body of an input clause along the order;
85:hardness is `DescriptiveComplexity.hornSat_PTIME_hard`, the Horn discharge. This is the
86:P-level analogue of the Cook–Levin theorem, and like it it is machine-free. -/
87:theorem HORNSAT_PTIME_complete : PTIME.Complete HORNSAT :=
88:  ⟨hornSat_mem_PTIME, hornSat_PTIME_hard⟩
89:
90:/-- **PTIME ⊆ NP**, i.e., `SigmaP 0 ⊆ SigmaP 1`: every SO-Horn definable problem
91:reduces to HORN-SAT, which is in NP. This is the level-0 case of
92:`DescriptiveComplexity.sigmaP_subset_sigmaP_succ`; it lives here rather than with the
93:hierarchy because it goes through the Horn discharge, needing no separate
94:compilation of a Horn program into an existential second-order sentence. -/
95:theorem PTIME_subset_NP : PTIME ⊆ NP := by
96:  intro L _ P hP
97:  obtain ⟨f⟩ := hornSat_hard_of_sigmaSOHornDefinable P hP
98:  exact NP.mem_of_orderedReduction f hornSat_mem_NP
99:
100:/-- **co-PTIME ⊆ coNP**, i.e., `PiP 0 ⊆ PiP 1`: the mirror of
101:`DescriptiveComplexity.PTIME_subset_NP` under complementation. -/
102:theorem coPTIME_subset_coNP : PiP 0 ⊆ PiP 1 := by
103:  intro L _ P hP
104:  rw [mem_piP_iff] at hP ⊢
105:  exact PTIME_subset_NP hP
106:
107:/-- **PTIME ⊆ coNP**, i.e., `SigmaP 0 ⊆ PiP 1`: complementing the Horn
108:discharge sends an SO-Horn definable problem to the complement of HORN-SAT,
109:which is in NP by the unsatisfiability certificate
110:`DescriptiveComplexity.hornSat_compl_mem_NP`. -/
111:theorem PTIME_subset_coNP : PTIME ⊆ coNP := by
112:  intro L _ P hP
113:  obtain ⟨f⟩ := hornSat_hard_of_sigmaSOHornDefinable P hP
114:  exact (mem_piP_iff 1 P).mpr (NP.mem_of_orderedReduction f.compl hornSat_compl_mem_NP)
115:
116:/-- **co-PTIME ⊆ NP**, i.e., `PiP 0 ⊆ SigmaP 1`: the mirror of
117:`DescriptiveComplexity.PTIME_subset_coNP`. -/
118:theorem coPTIME_subset_NP : PiP 0 ⊆ NP := by
119:  intro L _ P hP
120:  rw [mem_piP_iff] at hP
121:  obtain ⟨f⟩ := hornSat_hard_of_sigmaSOHornDefinable Pᶜ hP
122:  exact NP.mem_of_orderedReduction (f.compl.congrSource fun A _ _ => not_not)
123:    hornSat_compl_mem_NP

21:/-!
22:# Machine acceptance is NP-complete, and its deterministic restriction PTIME-complete
23:
24:Umbrella file for `DescriptiveComplexity.NTMAccept`, the problem “does this
25:nondeterministic Turing machine accept its input within as many steps as there
26:are positions?”, with the machine carried by the instance.
27:
28:The point of the problem is the machine bridge: every class
29:in this library is a definition in logic and every completeness theorem is
30:discharged by a first-order reduction, so that these classes really are *the*
31:NP and *the* P was, until this file, a citation. `NTMAccept` closes that gap
32:from inside the framework:
33:
34:* **membership** (`DescriptiveComplexity.ntmAccept_mem_NP`,
35:  `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Machine.Membership`) is Fagin's tableau argument – one
36:  existential block guesses the run, a first-order kernel checks it, and
37:  `DescriptiveComplexity.TMData.accepts_iff_exists_walk` turns an `ℕ`-indexed run into
38:  one indexed by the position elements, which is where the unary time bound is
39:  cashed in;
40:* **hardness** (`DescriptiveComplexity.ntmAccept_NP_hard`) is the reduction
41:  `SAT ≤ᶠᵒ[≤] NTMAccept`: a bespoke machine – guess an assignment in one sweep,
42:  check one clause per sweep, alternating direction – built *semantically* in
43:  `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Machine.Hardness` on the tape of
44:  `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Machine.Tape`, run by the phase machinery of
45:  `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Machine.Program`, and transcribed into defining
46:  formulas in `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Machine.Interp`.
47:
48:Two consequences are worth naming. `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NP_iff_le_ntmAccept` is
49:the machine characterization of the class: a problem is in NP – that is,
50:`Σ₁`-definable – exactly when it ordered-FO-reduces to machine acceptance.
51:And `DescriptiveComplexity.ntmAccept_reduces_to_sat` is the *textbook form* of the
52:Cook–Levin theorem – machine acceptance reduces to satisfiability – obtained
53:from the machine-free Tseitin discharge with no tableau-to-CNF encoding: the
54:membership proof already wrote the run as a `Σ₁` formula, and the generic
55:reduction to SAT applies to it like to any other. Conjoined with the hardness
56:direction, this gives `DescriptiveComplexity.ntmAccept_interreducible_sat` –
57:machine acceptance and satisfiability reduce to each other – the most faithful
58:representation of the Cook–Levin theorem this library offers.
59:`DescriptiveComplexity.SAT_complete_for_ntmAccept` states the same content with
60:the hardness half quantified over the class, which is SAT's NP-completeness for
61:the NP the *machine* defines and the form to compare with the mechanizations
62:that prove Cook–Levin over a machine model.
63:
64:As with any complexity-theoretic statement, these results are about finite
65:structures only
66:(`DescriptiveComplexity.ComplexityClass.mem_congr_finite`/`hard_congr_finite`).
67:-/

73:/-- Machine acceptance is NP-hard: SAT reduces to it by building the machine
74:`M_φ` inside the instance. -/
75:theorem ntmAccept_NP_hard : NP.Hard NTMAccept :=
76:  NP.hard_of_orderedReduction SatTM.sat_ordered_fo_reduction_ntmAccept sat_NP_hard
77:
78:/-- **Machine acceptance is NP-complete.** The classes of this library are
79:defined in logic; this theorem is the bridge saying its NP is the machine
80:one. -/
81:theorem ntmAccept_NP_complete : NP.Complete NTMAccept :=
82:  ⟨ntmAccept_mem_NP, ntmAccept_NP_hard⟩
83:
84:/-- **The machine characterization of NP**: a problem is `Σ₁`-definable exactly
85:when it ordered-FO-reduces to machine acceptance. Forward through SAT – the
86:generic Tseitin discharge followed by the machine of a CNF formula – and
87:backward because membership travels along reductions. -/
88:theorem mem_NP_iff_le_ntmAccept {L : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] (P : DecisionProblem L) :
89:    P ∈ NP ↔ Nonempty (P ≤ᶠᵒ[≤] NTMAccept) := by
90:  constructor
91:  · intro hP
92:    obtain ⟨g⟩ := sat_hard_of_sigmaSODefinable P hP
93:    exact ⟨g.trans SatTM.sat_ordered_fo_reduction_ntmAccept⟩
94:  · rintro ⟨f⟩
95:    exact NP.mem_of_orderedReduction f ntmAccept_mem_NP
96:
97:/-- **The textbook Cook–Levin theorem**: machine acceptance reduces to
98:satisfiability. No tableau-to-CNF encoding appears: the `Σ₁` definition of
99:acceptance feeds the machine-free Tseitin discharge. -/
100:theorem ntmAccept_reduces_to_sat : Nonempty (NTMAccept ≤ᶠᵒ[≤] SAT) :=
101:  sat_hard_of_sigmaSODefinable NTMAccept ntmAccept_sigmaSODefinable
102:
103:/-- **Machine acceptance and satisfiability are interreducible** – the most
104:faithful representation of the Cook–Levin theorem in this library, both
105:directions of the correspondence in one statement: acceptance reduces to
106:`DescriptiveComplexity.SAT` through the `Σ₁` definition of a run, and
107:`DescriptiveComplexity.SAT` reduces back by building the machine `M_φ`
108:inside the instance. -/
109:theorem ntmAccept_interreducible_sat :
110:    Nonempty (NTMAccept ≤ᶠᵒ[≤] SAT) ∧ Nonempty (SAT ≤ᶠᵒ[≤] NTMAccept) :=
111:  ⟨ntmAccept_reduces_to_sat, ⟨SatTM.sat_ordered_fo_reduction_ntmAccept⟩⟩
112:
113:/-- **`DescriptiveComplexity.SAT` is NP-complete, `NP` read as the machine
114:class**: satisfiability is accepted by a machine, and *every* problem accepted
115:by one reduces to it.
116:
117:This is `ntmAccept_interreducible_sat` with the hardness half quantified over
118:the class rather than stated at one problem, which is the form the mechanized
119:Cook–Levin literature proves; it is the statement to compare against, since
120:nothing here is definitional about the logically defined
121:`DescriptiveComplexity.NP` – the class it is complete for is the one the
122:machine defines. The extra content over the interreducible form is exactly the
123:cofinal quantifier: `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NP_iff_le_ntmAccept` turns an
124:arbitrary problem accepted by a machine into a `Σ₁` definition, which the
125:generic discharge then sends to `DescriptiveComplexity.SAT`. -/
126:theorem SAT_complete_for_ntmAccept :
127:    Nonempty (SAT ≤ᶠᵒ[≤] NTMAccept) ∧
128:      ∀ {L : Language.{0, 0}} [L.IsRelational] (P : DecisionProblem L),
129:        Nonempty (P ≤ᶠᵒ[≤] NTMAccept) → Nonempty (P ≤ᶠᵒ[≤] SAT) :=
130:  ⟨⟨SatTM.sat_ordered_fo_reduction_ntmAccept⟩,
131:    fun P h => sat_hard_of_sigmaSODefinable P ((mem_NP_iff_le_ntmAccept P).mpr h)⟩

744:<a href="https://archive.softwareheritage.org/browse/origin/?origin_url=https://github.com/PierreSenellart/descriptive-complexity" rel="nofollow"><img src="https://camo.githubusercontent.com/23230675e61028566a588051ee59de7c202d776e1b8cf0ba257a2a6140e4a8a8/68747470733a2f2f617263686976652e736f66747761726568657269746167652e6f72672f62616467652f6f726967696e2f68747470733a2f2f6769746875622e636f6d2f50696572726553656e656c6c6172742f64657363726970746976652d636f6d706c65786974792f" alt="Archived in Software Heritage" data-canonical-src="https://archive.softwareheritage.org/badge/origin/https://github.com/PierreSenellart/descriptive-complexity/" style="max-width: 100%;"></a></p>
745:<p dir="auto">A Lean 4 library for descriptive complexity on top of Mathlib's <code>ModelTheory</code>,
746:in the style of Immerman (<em>Descriptive Complexity</em>, ch. 3). Every complexity
747:class is defined logically, so membership, hardness and completeness proofs
748:need no machine model: a definability witness for membership, a first-order
749:reduction for hardness, and the framework closes them into a <code>Complete</code>
750:theorem. All declarations live in the <code>DescriptiveComplexity</code> namespace.</p>

1:# DescriptiveComplexity
2:
3:[![CI](https://github.com/PierreSenellart/descriptive-complexity/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=master)](https://github.com/PierreSenellart/descriptive-complexity/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
4:[![Mathlib](https://img.shields.io/badge/Mathlib-v4.33.0-blue)](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/releases/tag/v4.33.0)
5:[![DOI](https://img.shields.io/badge/DOI-10.5281%2Fzenodo.21678423-007ec6)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21678423)
6:[![Archived in Software Heritage](https://archive.softwareheritage.org/badge/origin/https://github.com/PierreSenellart/descriptive-complexity/)](https://archive.softwareheritage.org/browse/origin/?origin_url=https://github.com/PierreSenellart/descriptive-complexity)
7:
8:A Lean 4 library for descriptive complexity on top of Mathlib's `ModelTheory`,
9:in the style of Immerman (*Descriptive Complexity*, ch. 3). Every complexity
10:class is defined logically, so membership, hardness and completeness proofs
11:need no machine model: a definability witness for membership, a first-order
12:reduction for hardness, and the framework closes them into a `Complete`
13:theorem. All declarations live in the `DescriptiveComplexity` namespace.
14:
15:Complexity theory is essentially absent from Mathlib because formalizing a
16:model of computation with resource bounds is hard. Most classical hardness
17:reductions do not need the full power of PTIME: they are first-order
18:expressible. An FO reduction is computable in AC⁰ ⊆ LOGSPACE ⊆ PTIME, so
19:exhibiting one is a stronger statement than exhibiting a Karp reduction, while
20:requiring only first-order logic, which Mathlib already has.
21:
22:## Three layers
23:
24:* **Model theory.** A decision problem is an isomorphism-invariant property of
25:  finite structures over a chosen vocabulary. Concrete instance types can be
26:  used instead: a bundled `Encoding` requires polynomial size bounds in both
27:  directions to construct, and computable `Decoding`s read well-formed
28:  structures back, so completeness theorems can be restricted to the non-junk
29:  instances.
30:* **Complexity classes.** Classes are logically defined and closed under FO
31:  reductions by construction: the polynomial hierarchy by second-order
32:  quantifier alternation, PTIME by the Horn fragment, NL by the Krom fragment,
33:  PSPACE by second-order transitive closure, RE by value invention, with the
34:  fixed-point logics FO(LFP)/FO(IFP)/FO(PFP) alongside. Machine models are
35:  theorems here, not definitions (see the table below). The downward closure
36:  `below Q₀` of a fixed problem is itself a class, which expresses
37:  “GI-complete” without any logic.
38:* **Reductions.** Tagged `dim`-dimensional first-order interpretations between
39:  languages give the reduction `≤ᶠᵒ`, with its order-invariant variant `≤ᶠᵒ[≤]`
40:  for gadgets that genuinely need a linear order and a relativized variant
41:  `≤ʳᶠᵒ[≤]` for problems whose target domain is definable; all are closed under
42:  composition. The problem catalog is one problem per file – vocabulary,
43:  reductions, completeness theorem – with tutorial-style worked examples.
44:
45:## Results
46:
47:* Cook–Levin, without a machine model (`SAT_NP_complete`), and all of Karp's 21
48:  problems.
49:* The Immerman–Vardi theorem (`lfpDefinable_iff_mem_PTIME`) and the
50:  Abiteboul–Vianu theorem
51:  (`ifpDefinableFree_eq_pfpDefinableFree_iff_ptime_eq_pspace`).
52:* Machine bridges: a problem is in the library's NP (resp. PTIME) exactly when
53:  it ordered-FO-reduces to acceptance by a nondeterministic (resp.
54:  deterministic) polynomial-time Turing machine (`mem_NP_iff_le_ntmAccept`,
55:  `mem_PTIME_iff_le_dtmAccept`).
56:* Lower bounds, none of them conditional on a complexity assumption:
57:  Ehrenfeucht–Fraïssé games on finite structures, and the inexpressibility of
58:  EVEN even when the sentence is given a linear order (`even_not_foDefinable`),
59:  whence `FO ⊊ FO(TC)` (`exists_tcDefinable_not_foDefinable`) and, since EVEN is
60:  definable once formulas may add ranks, `FO(≤) ⊊ AC⁰`
61:  (`exists_ac0Definable_not_foDefinable`). The same problem shows, by the
62:  `k`-pebble game, that order-free FO(IFP) does not capture PTIME
63:  (`exists_mem_PTIME_not_ifpDefinableFree`), so the linear order in the capture
64:  theorems cannot be dropped.
65:* AC⁰ is read here as the logic `FO(≤, +, ×)`; no circuit model is involved. It
66:  is proved to sit inside L (`ac0Definable_mem_LOGSPACE`), by a deterministic
67:  multi-head automaton that computes the numeric predicates instead of reading
68:  them, and to equal both `FO(≤, BIT)` and its machine model, logarithmic time
69:  with constantly many alternations (`ac0Definable_iff_ltDecidable`: both halves
70:  of Immerman's Thm 1.17, Bit Sum Lemma included). That machine class is the
71:  logarithmic-time hierarchy, not the larger ALOGTIME of unbounded alternation.
72:
73:## Complexity classes and complete problems
74:
75:Each problem listed is proved complete for its class: both a member, and hard
76:for it under FO reductions.
77:
78:| Complexity class | Logical characterization | Machine model | Problems proved complete |
79:| --- | --- | --- | --- |
80:| **L** = LOGSPACE | FO(≤, DTC) | deterministic two-way `k`-head automaton | REACHd · UNREACHd |
81:| **NL** | SO-Krom(≤); equivalently FO(≤, TC) | two-way `k`-head automaton | REACH · UNREACH · 2SAT |
82:| **PTIME** = Σ₀ᵖ = Π₀ᵖ | SO-Horn(≤); equivalently FO(≤, LFP) or FO(≤, IFP) | deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine | HORN-SAT · CVP (circuit value) · GAME (alternating reachability) · acceptance by a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine |
83:| **NP** = Σ₁ᵖ | ∃SO; equivalently ∃SO[new, d], value invention bounded by the instance's `d`-tuples | nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machine | **SAT-family:** SAT · 3SAT · NAE-SAT · NAE-3SAT · 1-in-SAT<br>**Coloring:** 3-Colorability · `k`-Colorability (`k ≥ 3`) · Chromatic Number · Clique Cover<br>**Cliques & subgraphs:** Clique · Independent Set · Vertex Cover · Subgraph Isomorphism<br>**Sets & hypergraphs:** Set Cover · Hitting Set · Set Packing · Exact Cover · Set Splitting · Dominating Set · 3-Dimensional Matching<br>**Graphs:** Feedback Vertex Set · Feedback Arc Set · Steiner Tree (node- & edge-weighted) · Max Cut · Hamilton Circuit (directed & undirected)<br>**Numbers (in binary):** Knapsack · Partition · 0-1 Integer Programming · Job Sequencing<br>**Machines:** acceptance by a nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machine |
84:| **coNP** = Π₁ᵖ | ∀SO | the same machine, accepting when *every* run does | TAUT · 3-DNF-TAUT · 3-UNSAT · acceptance by such a machine |
85:| **DP** | a Σ₁ and a Π₁ sentence conjoined | – | SAT-UNSAT |
86:| **Σₖᵖ** (`k ≥ 1`) | Σₖ¹: `k` alternating second-order quantifier blocks, existential first | alternating polynomial-time Turing machine, `k` blocks, existential first | `QBF k` (quantified Boolean formulas, `k` blocks) · acceptance by such a machine |
87:| **Πₖᵖ** (`k ≥ 1`) | Πₖ¹: `k` alternating second-order quantifier blocks, universal first | the same machine, universal first | `QBF∀ k` (universal-first, `k` blocks) · acceptance by such a machine |
88:| **PH** | SO | – | – |
89:| **PSPACE** | SO(TC); equivalently FO(≤, PFP) | polynomial-space Turing machine, deterministic or not | SUCCINCT-REACH · QSAT · acceptance by a space-bounded Turing machine (deterministic & not) |
90:| **EXPTIME** | SO(LFP), i.e., PTIME read over an exponential expansion; equivalently SO-GAME, a second-order alternating game | alternating polynomial-space Turing machine | acceptance by such a machine (`APSPACE = EXPTIME`) |
91:| **NEXPTIME** | ∃SO over an exponential expansion (NP read there); equivalently ∃SO[new, exp], value invention bounded exponentially | wide machine, clocked | acceptance by such a machine within its clock · tiling a wide square (the `2ⁿ × 2ⁿ` tiling) |
92:| **EXPSPACE** | SO(PFP), i.e., PSPACE read over an exponential expansion | wide machine, space-bounded | acceptance by such a machine in bounded space (deterministic & not) · tiling a wide corridor (width `2ⁿ`, unbounded height) |
93:| **RE** | ∃SO[new] (∃SO with value invention, unbounded) | Turing machine, no step or space bound | FINSAT (Trakhtenbrot's theorem) · CODEHALT · HALT · PCP (Post's correspondence problem) |
94:| **the degree of a problem** – `below Q₀`, e.g., **GI** | none: a downward closure under FO reductions rather than a logic | – | for GI: Graph Isomorphism · Digraph Isomorphism · DAG Isomorphism |
95:
96:Two of the models are named rather than described: both head automata walk a
97:linear order of the universe, and a *wide* machine carries its control in the
98:instance while its tape is addressed by an exponential expansion of it. Each
99:entry of the machine column is an equivalence proved here between the logical
100:definition and acceptance by that model. The classes are also matched against
101:Mathlib's computability layer: RE is recursive enumerability, every RE-hard
102:problem is undecidable, and RE ≠ co-RE.
103:
104:The last row states completeness against a problem instead of a logic, which is
105:what “GI-complete” means. It agrees with the logical definitions where both
106:apply: `NP = below SAT`, `PTIME = below HORN-SAT` and their siblings are
107:theorems, so SAT-hardness is NP-hardness.
108:
109:## Scope
110:
111:These limitations are *intrinsic* to the machine-free approach; for what is
112:merely not built yet, see `ROADMAP.md`.
113:
114:* **Complexity of problems, not of algorithms.** No cost model, no `O(·)`, no
115:  fine-grained complexity: what you prove is membership, hardness and
116:  completeness for the coarse classes above.
117:* **Instances are finite relational structures, not strings.** From PTIME up,
118:  the machine bridges characterize the classes from inside the framework, by
119:  acceptance problems whose instances carry the machine; at L, NL and AC⁰ a
120:  single machine, fixed once, decides every instance. Either way their agreement
121:  with the usual presentations over string encodings is classical (Fagin;
122:  Immerman–Vardi) and is not formalized here – except for RE, where
123:  `mem_RE_iff_rePred` identifies the class with Mathlib's `REPred` on an
124:  encoding of finite structures.
125:* **The reduction must be expressible in logic.** A poly-time reduction that is
126:  not FO-expressible cannot be used; gadgets often need a linear order, tags or
127:  extra dimensions, and arithmetic inside formulas is limited (addition and
128:  comparison are FO(≤); multiplication is not FO).
129:* **Completeness and structure, not class separations.** Whether P = NP and the
130:  like is open mathematics the framework does not decide. Separations between
131:  *logics* are in scope, and proved (see above).
132:
133:## Related projects
134:
135:* **[Complexitylib](https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/complexitylib)** (Lean 4
136:  and Mathlib) is machine-model-first: `P` and `NP` are defined by time-bounded
137:  multi-tape Turing machines, and hardness is a polynomial-time many-one
138:  reduction exhibited as a machine. It reaches results out of scope here, notably
139:  the deterministic time hierarchy theorem and circuit lower bounds; its complete
140:  problems are SAT and 3SAT. Its descriptive-complexity component was developed
141:  independently of this library, on its own foundations rather than Mathlib's
142:  `ModelTheory`.
143:* **[Karp21](https://github.com/wimmers/poly-reductions)** (Isabelle/HOL)
144:  formalizes polynomial-time reductions between Karp's problems, with running
145:  times accounted for in NREST; the public repository covers about eight of the 21.
146:* **The Cook–Levin theorem** is mechanized against concrete models of computation
147:  by [Gäher and Kunze, ITP 2021](https://uds-psl.github.io/cook-levin/) in
148:  Coq/Rocq (call-by-value λ-calculus) and [Balbach, AFP
149:  2023](https://www.isa-afp.org/entries/Cook_Levin.html) in Isabelle/HOL
150:  (two-tape oblivious Turing machines). Here (`SAT_NP_complete`) it is proved for
151:  the logically defined `NP`, the identification with the machine class being a
152:  separate theorem.
153:* **[Cookbook reductions](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.MFCS.2024.56)** (Grange,
154:  Vehlken, Vortmeier and Zeume, MFCS 2024) also specify reductions in first-order
155:  logic, but check them automatically in a teaching setting rather than in an
156:  interactive theorem prover.
157:
158:## Use as a dependency
159:
160:Lake builds a single Mathlib per workspace, so pick the release whose Mathlib
161:pin is the *same* as your project's, not merely a compatible one.
162:
163:| DescriptiveComplexity | Mathlib | Toolchain |
164:| --- | --- | --- |
165:| `v1.2.0` | `v4.33.0` | `leanprover/lean4:v4.33.0` |
166:| `v1.1.0` | `v4.33.0-rc1` | `leanprover/lean4:v4.33.0-rc1` |
167:| `v1.0.0` | `v4.33.0-rc1` | `leanprover/lean4:v4.33.0-rc1` |
168:| `master` | latest pin, moves | see `lean-toolchain` |
169:
170:Version numbers are the library's own and follow [semantic
171:versioning](https://semver.org/); the `lean-toolchain` file at each tag is
172:authoritative for the pin. A **patch** release keeps the Mathlib pin it was cut
173:against, and **a new pin always takes at least a minor bump** – so depend on
174:`~1.0.0`, which stays within a single pin, rather than on `^1.0.0`.
175:
176:The package is indexed on
177:[Reservoir](https://reservoir.lean-lang.org/@PierreSenellart/descriptive-complexity),
178:so it can be required by name. In a `lakefile.toml`:
179:
180:```toml
181:[[require]]
182:name = "descriptive-complexity"
183:scope = "PierreSenellart"
184:version = "~1.2.0"
185:```
186:
187:or, in a `lakefile.lean`:
188:
189:```lean
190:require "PierreSenellart" / "descriptive-complexity" @ "~1.2.0"
191:```
192:
193:What follows `@` is a version *range*, not a version: Lake rejects a bare
194:number there.
195:
196:To pin a commit, or to follow `master`, require it from git instead:
197:
198:```toml
199:[[require]]
200:name = "descriptive-complexity"
201:git = "https://github.com/PierreSenellart/descriptive-complexity"
202:rev = "v1.2.0"
203:```
204:
205:```lean
206:require "descriptive-complexity" from git
207:  "https://github.com/PierreSenellart/descriptive-complexity" @ "v1.2.0"
208:```
209:
210:Pin a version tag or a commit hash rather than `master`, for reproducible
211:builds. Then `import DescriptiveComplexity` brings in the whole library; import
212:individual modules (for instance `DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Sat`) to keep
213:build times down.
214:
215:## Documentation
216:
217:* **API reference**:
218:  <https://pierresenellart.github.io/descriptive-complexity/DescriptiveComplexity.html>
219:  – the `DescriptiveComplexity` module page is a part-by-part map of the library,
220:  and every declaration is documented on its own page. Rebuilt from `master` on
221:  every push.
222:* **Tutorials**: `DescriptiveComplexity/Examples/ConjunctiveQueries.lean` and
223:  `DescriptiveComplexity/Examples/GraphCrawling.lean`, worked examples read top
224:  to bottom, each walking through a new problem domain in the order a user meets
225:  it (concrete problem → encoding → vocabulary and semantics → faithfulness →
226:  membership → hardness → completeness).
227:* **Planned work**: `ROADMAP.md` – classes beyond PSPACE, counting and
228:  optimization problems, more inexpressibility results, finer reduction notions.

1875:## The problem catalog
1876:
1877:`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems` holds one decision problem per file, each with
1878:its vocabulary, FO reductions and a completeness theorem. Every class in the
1879:table below is *defined* logically; each problem listed is proved **complete**
1880:for it – both a member and hard under FO reductions. The catalog covers all of
1881:Karp's 21 NP-complete problems. Each problem's own module page documents its
1882:reduction and certificate in full.
1883:
1884:| Complexity class | Logical characterization | Machine model | Problems proved complete |
1885:| --- | --- | --- | --- |
1886:| `LOGSPACE` (`L`) | FO(≤, DTC): first-order logic with a deterministic transitive closure, over a linearly ordered universe | deterministic two-way `k`-head automaton † | REACHd · UNREACHd |
1887:| `NL` | SO-Krom(≤): ∃SO with a Krom kernel, at most two second-order literals per clause; equivalently FO(≤, TC), first-order logic with a transitive closure – both over a linearly ordered universe | two-way `k`-head automaton † | REACH · UNREACH · 2SAT |
1888:| `PTIME` = `Σ₀ᵖ` = `Π₀ᵖ` | SO-Horn(≤): ∃SO with a Horn kernel; equivalently FO(≤, LFP), first-order logic with a least fixed point – both over a linearly ordered universe | deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine | HORN-SAT · CVP |
1889:| `NP` = `Σ₁ᵖ` | ∃SO: existential second-order logic | nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machine | **SAT-family:** SAT · 3SAT · NAE-SAT · NAE-3SAT · 1-in-SAT<br>**Coloring:** 3-Colorability · `k`-Colorability (`k ≥ 3`) · Chromatic Number · Clique Cover<br>**Cliques & subgraphs:** Clique · Independent Set · Vertex Cover · Subgraph Isomorphism<br>**Sets & hypergraphs:** Set Cover · Hitting Set · Set Packing · Exact Cover · Set Splitting · Dominating Set · 3-Dimensional Matching<br>**Graphs:** Feedback Vertex Set · Feedback Arc Set · Steiner Tree (node- & edge-weighted) · Max Cut · Hamilton Circuit (directed & undirected)<br>**Numbers (in binary):** Knapsack · Partition · 0-1 Integer Programming · Job Sequencing<br>**Machines:** acceptance by a nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machine |
1890:| `coNP` = `Π₁ᵖ` | ∀SO: universal second-order logic | the same machine, accepting when *every* run does | TAUT · 3-DNF-TAUT · 3-UNSAT (and QBF∀ at one block) · `ATMAccept 1 false` |
1891:| `DP` | a `Σ₁` and a `Π₁` sentence conjoined | — | SAT-UNSAT |
1892:| `Σₖᵖ` (`k ≥ 1`) | `Σₖ¹`: `k` alternating second-order quantifier blocks, existential first | alternating polynomial-time Turing machine, `k` blocks, existential first | `QBF k` – at `k = 1`, NP · `ATMAccept k true` |
1893:| `Πₖᵖ` (`k ≥ 1`) | `Πₖ¹`: `k` alternating second-order quantifier blocks, universal first | the same machine, universal first | `QBF∀ k` – at `k = 1`, coNP · `ATMAccept k false` |
1894:| `PH` | full second-order logic | — | — |
1895:| `PSPACE` | SO(TC): second-order logic with a transitive closure over assignments of a block of relation variables | polynomial-space Turing machine, deterministic or not | SUCCINCT-REACH · QSAT · space-bounded machine acceptance (deterministic & not) |
1896:| `EXPTIME` | SO(LFP): PTIME read over an exponential expansion; equivalently SO-GAME, a second-order alternating game | alternating polynomial-space Turing machine | acceptance by such a machine (`APSPACE = EXPTIME`) |
1897:| `NEXPTIME` | ∃SO over an exponential expansion, i.e., NP read there; equivalently ∃SO[new, exp], value invention bounded exponentially | wide machine, clocked | acceptance by such a machine within its clock · tiling a wide square (the `2ⁿ × 2ⁿ` tiling) |
1898:| `EXPSPACE` | SO(PFP): PSPACE read over an exponential expansion | wide machine, space-bounded | acceptance by such a machine in bounded space (deterministic & not) · tiling a wide corridor (width `2ⁿ`, unbounded height) |
1899:| `RE` | ∃SO[new]: ∃SO with value invention, the relation variables ranging over the universe extended by finitely many invented values | Turing machine, no step or space bound | FINSAT (Trakhtenbrot's theorem) · CODEHALT · HALT · PCP (Post's correspondence problem) |
1900:| the degree of a problem: `DescriptiveComplexity.ComplexityClass.below Q₀`, e.g., `GI` | none – a downward closure under `≤ᶠᵒ[≤]` rather than a logic, which is the point of the construction | — | for `GI`: Graph Isomorphism · Digraph Isomorphism · DAG Isomorphism |
1901:
1902:Two of the models are named rather than described: both head automata walk a
1903:linear order of the universe, and a *wide* machine carries its control in the
1904:instance while its tape is addressed by an exponential expansion of it
1905:(`DescriptiveComplexity.Problems.Wide`).
1906:
1907:Each entry of the **machine model** column is an equivalence *proved here*
1908:between the logical definition of the class and acceptance by that model:
1909:`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_LOGSPACE_iff_automaton` and
1910:`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NL_iff_automaton` (†), and, through the completeness
1911:of an acceptance problem, `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_PTIME_iff_le_dtmAccept`,
1912:`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NP_iff_le_ntmAccept`,
1913:`DescriptiveComplexity.le_dtmAcceptSpace_of_mem_PSPACE`,
1914:`DescriptiveComplexity.atmAcceptSpace_EXPTIME_complete`,
1915:`DescriptiveComplexity.wideRegAccept_NEXPTIME_complete`,
1916:`DescriptiveComplexity.wideAcceptSpace_EXPSPACE_complete` and
1917:`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_RE_iff_rePred`. A dash marks a class for which no
1918:such equivalence is proved here.
1919:
1920:† Capture theorems, both directions: `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NL_iff_automaton`
1921:for `NL`, and `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_LOGSPACE_iff_automaton` for `LOGSPACE`,
1922:where the machine is required to be deterministic.
1923:
1924:Headline results and cross-references:
1925:
1926:* **Cook–Levin, machine-free** (`DescriptiveComplexity.SAT_NP_complete`;
1927:  [Cook 1971][cook1971complexity]; [Levin 1973][levin1973universal]): SAT is
1928:  NP-complete by a Tseitin discharge, no machine model. 3-colorability is
1929:  FO-interreducible with SAT in both directions.
1930:* **The machine bridge**: machine acceptance
1931:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.NTMAccept`) – does this nondeterministic Turing
1932:  machine, carried as data by the instance, accept its input within a
1933:  polynomial step budget (as many steps as there are tape positions)? – is
1934:  NP-complete
1935:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.ntmAccept_NP_complete`), so a problem is in the
1936:  library's NP exactly when it ordered-FO-reduces to it
1937:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_NP_iff_le_ntmAccept`): the logically defined
1938:  class *is* the machine one. The textbook Cook–Levin – machine acceptance
1939:  reduces to SAT – is `DescriptiveComplexity.ntmAccept_reduces_to_sat`. One
1940:  level down, the *deterministic* restriction
1941:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.DTMAccept`, a functional transition table folded into
1942:  the yes-instances) is PTIME-complete
1943:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.dtmAccept_PTIME_complete`): membership because a
1944:  deterministic run is a least fixed point, read through the formalized
1945:  FO(LFP) → SO-Horn translation, and hardness by a unit-propagation machine
1946:  built inside the HORN-SAT instance – so PTIME, too, is the machine class
1947:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.mem_PTIME_iff_le_dtmAccept`), with the Grädel-side
1948:  textbook discharge `DescriptiveComplexity.dtmAccept_reduces_to_hornSat`.
1949:* **The machine bridge for the hierarchy**: the same identification one level
1950:  of alternation at a time. `DescriptiveComplexity.ATMAccept k start` – does
1951:  this *alternating* machine, whose states carry `k` block marks entered in
1952:  order, accept its input within the same unary budget? – is `Σₖᵖ`-complete for
1953:  an existential first block
1954:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.atmAccept_sigmaP_complete`) and `Πₖᵖ`-complete for a
1955:  universal one (`DescriptiveComplexity.atmAccept_piP_complete`), so each level
1956:  of the logically defined hierarchy is the corresponding level of the
1957:  alternating-machine hierarchy of [Chandra–Kozen–Stockmeyer
1958:  1981][chandra1981alternation]. At one block the two are the nondeterministic
1959:  model and its dual, which is where coNP gets its machine
1960:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.atmAccept_one_complete`,
1961:  `DescriptiveComplexity.atmAccept_one_coNP_complete`,
1962:  `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_sigmaP_iff_le_atmAccept`,
1963:  `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_piP_iff_le_atmAccept`). Membership reads a run as
1964:  a `k`-round game, each round guessing one walk; hardness builds the machine
1965:  `M_φ` of a quantified Boolean formula inside the instance – one sweep of the
1966:  tape per quantifier block, whose only choice is which of its block's
1967:  variables to set, so that the moves of a round *are* the truth assignments of
1968:  its block, followed by a deterministic check phase walking the clauses.
1969:* **All of Karp's 21** ([Karp 1972][karp1972reducibility]): the SAT, clique,
1970:  set, coloring, graph and number families above, closed by the two Hamilton
1971:  circuit problems – a circuit read as a linear order of the universe, hard
1972:  from Vertex Cover by Karp's twelve-vertex cover-testing gadget.
1973:* **CVP, the textbook `PTIME`-complete problem**
1974:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.CVP_PTIME_complete`; [Ladner
1975:  1975][ladner1975circuit]): membership is an FO(LFP) definition – the problem's
1976:  semantics *is* a least fixed point, so the rule system is the gate rules
1977:  transcribed and the output sentence is the one a Horn program cannot write,
1978:  “the output gate is in the true rail”. Hardness draws the unit-propagation
1979:  circuit inside a HORN-SAT instance and reports the *failure* of Horn
1980:  satisfiability, which keeps the circuit monotone and costs nothing, polynomial
1981:  time being closed under complement. The stages of the fixed point are unrolled
1982:  along the order and the two unbounded quantifiers of a round become chains of
1983:  fan-in-two gates; what makes it work is that the *wiring*, being defined by a
1984:  formula, may test where a literal occurs, where a fixed circuit may not.
1985:* **PTIME by the Horn fragment**: HORN-SAT is PTIME-complete
1986:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.HORNSAT_PTIME_complete`) by the Horn discharge and a
1987:  Horn program for unit propagation – the P-level analogue of Cook–Levin,
1988:  equally machine-free. REACH/UNREACH is a second worked instance of the
1989:  fragment, and a third one of the Krom fragment:
1990:  `DescriptiveComplexity.unreach_mem_NL` defines UNREACH by a two-literal
1991:  program guessing the vertices from which a marked target is reachable. In
1992:  both fragments it is the *complement* that is definable head-on, clauses
1993:  being able to close and to reject but not to force minimality; REACH escapes
1994:  at the Horn level through FO(LFP), and at the Krom level through `NL = coNL`
1995:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.reach_mem_NL`).
1996:* **Immerman–Vardi, `PTIME = FO(≤, LFP)`**
1997:  (`DescriptiveComplexity.lfpDefinable_iff_mem_PTIME`; [Vardi
1998:  1982][vardi1982complexity]; [Immerman 1986][immerman1986relational]): a problem is
1999:  in polynomial time exactly when a least-fixed-point definition computes it over a
2000:  linearly ordered universe – order-*invariantly*, since
2001:  `DescriptiveComplexity.LFPDefinable` asks for the equivalence at every linear order.
2002:  The class being *defined* by the Horn fragment, the content is the pair of
2003:  translations of `DescriptiveComplexity.FixedPointHorn`, so the theorem is
2004:  machine-free like everything else here; the machine reading is the bridge
2005:  `DescriptiveComplexity.mem_PTIME_iff_le_dtmAccept`. The inflationary variant
2006:  `DescriptiveComplexity.ifpDefinable_iff_mem_PTIME` is the same statement for
2007:  FO(≤, IFP), and `DescriptiveComplexity.hornSat_hard_of_lfpDefinable` is the
2008:  hardness discharge from the logic – a hardness proof may start from a fixed-point
2009:  definition, where negation is free, rather than from a Horn program.
2010:* **L by deterministic transitive closure**: REACHd – reachability along
FILE DescriptiveComplexity/Problems/Even.lean 90-140
90:/-! ### EVEN is not first-order
91:
92:The two witnesses are `Fin (2 * n + 2)` and `Fin (2 * n + 3)`: of different
93:parity, and both larger than the quantifier rank `n` that would have to tell
94:them apart. -/
95:
96:/-- **EVEN is not first-order definable.** A defining sentence of quantifier
97:rank `n` would have to separate two bare sets of at least `n` elements each,
98:which the duplicator's strategy (`DescriptiveComplexity.efEquiv_bare`)
99:forbids. -/
100:theorem even_not_foDefinableFree : ¬FODefinableFree EVEN := by
101:  intro h
102:  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := exists_card_bound_of_foDefinableFree h
103:  let : Language.empty.Structure (Fin (2 * N + 2)) := Language.emptyStructure
104:  let : Language.empty.Structure (Fin (2 * N + 3)) := Language.emptyStructure
105:  have hcard₁ : Nat.card (Fin (2 * N + 2)) = 2 * N + 2 := by simp
106:  have hcard₂ : Nat.card (Fin (2 * N + 3)) = 2 * N + 3 := by simp
107:  have hiff := hN (Fin (2 * N + 2)) (Fin (2 * N + 3)) (by omega) (by omega)
108:  rw [even_holds_iff, even_holds_iff, hcard₁, hcard₂] at hiff
109:  have h₁ : Even (2 * N + 2) := ⟨N + 1, by omega⟩
110:  have h₂ : ¬Even (2 * N + 3) := by
111:    rintro ⟨m, hm⟩
112:    omega
113:  exact h₂ (hiff.mp h₁)
114:
115:/-! ### EVEN is not first-order even with an order
116:
117:The order-free result above says little on its own: a bare set carries no
118:information beyond its size, and a sentence of quantifier rank `n` sees that
119:size only up to `n`. The order-invariant statement is the real theorem – the
120:structure now *does* determine every point's position, and the sentence may
121:speak about it – and it needs Ehrenfeucht's theorem
122:(`DescriptiveComplexity.efEquiv_linearOrder`), whose bound is exponential
123:rather than linear in the quantifier rank. -/
124:
125:/-- **EVEN is not first-order definable, even order-invariantly**: no sentence
126:over the ordered expansion defines it, however it uses the order. A defining
127:sentence of quantifier rank `n` would have to separate two finite linear
128:orders of `2 ^ n * 2` and `2 ^ n * 2 + 1` elements, which the duplicator's
129:strategy on a line (`DescriptiveComplexity.efEquiv_linearOrder`) forbids.
130:
131:Together with `DescriptiveComplexity.even_tcDefinable` below, this is the
132:unconditional strict inclusion `FO ⊊ FO(TC)`, and, through the inclusions the
133:library proves for the classes above `DescriptiveComplexity.NL`, the statement
134:that first-order logic is strictly weaker than every logic here. -/
135:theorem even_not_foDefinable : ¬FODefinable EVEN := by
136:  rintro ⟨φ, hφ⟩
137:  set n := qdepth φ with hn
138:  have hpow : 0 < 2 ^ n := Nat.two_pow_pos n
139:  let : Language.empty.Structure (Fin (2 ^ n * 2)) := Language.emptyStructure
140:  let : Language.empty.Structure (Fin (2 ^ n * 2 + 1)) := Language.emptyStructure
FILE DescriptiveComplexity/Problems/Even.lean 315-425
315:
316:/-- **`FO ⊊ FO(TC)`, unconditionally.** First-order logic with a transitive
317:closure is *strictly* stronger than first-order logic on ordered finite
318:structures: the inclusion is `DescriptiveComplexity.FODefinable.tcDefinable`,
319:and EVEN separates the two – a single walk along the order defines it, and no
320:sentence does. No complexity-theoretic assumption enters either half. -/
321:theorem exists_tcDefinable_not_foDefinable :
322:    ∃ P : DecisionProblem Language.empty, TCDefinable P ∧ ¬FODefinable P :=
323:  ⟨EVEN, even_tcDefinable, even_not_foDefinable⟩
324:
325:/-- **EVEN is in NL** – as far from first-order logic as it is easy to
326:compute. -/
327:theorem even_mem_NL : EVEN ∈ NL :=
328:  (tcDefinable_iff_mem_NL EVEN).mp even_tcDefinable
329:
330:/-- **EVEN is in PTIME**. -/
331:theorem even_mem_PTIME : EVEN ∈ PTIME :=
332:  NL_subset_PTIME even_mem_NL
333:
334:/-! ### EVEN is AC⁰: the numeric predicates see the size of the universe
335:
336:No walk is needed either. A bare set carries no information beyond its size,
337:and the size is exactly what the numeric predicates of
338:`DescriptiveComplexity.Arithmetic` make visible: the greatest element has rank
339:`Nat.card A - 1`, so the universe is even precisely when nothing doubles to it
340:(`DescriptiveComplexity.evenCardSentence`, one `∀` and one `∃`, using addition
341:only). With `DescriptiveComplexity.even_not_foDefinable` this gives
342:`FO(≤) ⊊ AC⁰` outright.
343:
344:**This says nothing about PARITY.** EVEN asks the parity of the *universe* –
345:of the input's length, which a circuit family is indexed by and a sentence with
346:`+` reads off the top rank. PARITY asks the parity of a *marked subset*, part of
347:the input, and that is the problem outside AC⁰ by the switching lemma. The two
348:must not be confused: nothing here bears on the second, and this library proves
349:no AC⁰ lower bound. -/
350:
351:/-- **EVEN is AC⁰ definable**: the greatest element has rank `Nat.card A - 1`,
352:so the universe has an even number of elements exactly when no element doubles
353:to the greatest one – the sentence `DescriptiveComplexity.evenCardSentence`,
354:which mentions the input vocabulary not at all.
355:
356:Contrast with PARITY, the parity of a marked *subset*, which is classically
357:*not* in AC⁰: see the section docstring. -/
358:theorem even_ac0Definable : AC0Definable EVEN :=
359:  ⟨evenCardSentence Language.empty, fun A _ _ _ _ =>
360:    (even_holds_iff A).trans (realize_evenCardSentence A).symm⟩
361:
362:/-- **`FO(≤) ⊊ AC⁰`, unconditionally.** First-order logic with the numeric
363:predicates is *strictly* stronger than first-order logic with a bare linear
364:order: the inclusion is `DescriptiveComplexity.FODefinable.ac0Definable`, and
365:EVEN separates the two – addition reads the parity of the top rank, and no
366:sentence over the order alone defines it, however it uses the order. No
367:complexity-theoretic assumption enters either half.
368:
369:This is the second unconditional separation of the library, beside
370:`DescriptiveComplexity.exists_tcDefinable_not_foDefinable`, and it is the one
371:that says the arithmetic is not decoration. -/
372:theorem exists_ac0Definable_not_foDefinable :
373:    ∃ P : DecisionProblem Language.empty, AC0Definable P ∧ ¬FODefinable P :=
374:  ⟨EVEN, even_ac0Definable, even_not_foDefinable⟩
375:
376:/-! ### Order-free FO(IFP) does not capture PTIME
377:
378:The order-invariant capture theorem `lfpDefinable_iff_mem_PTIME` says that
379:over *ordered* structures a least fixed point defines exactly the polynomial
380:time properties. Drop the order and the inflationary logic – which is the same
381:logic there – no longer reaches all of PTIME, and EVEN is the witness: a
382:`k`-variable induction cannot count past `k` pebbles, and two bare sets with
383:`k` elements each are `k`-pebble equivalent whatever their sizes
384:(`DescriptiveComplexity.equivK₂_bare`). -/
385:
386:/-- **EVEN is not order-free FO(IFP) definable**: a defining induction with
387:variable budget `k` – covering also the quantifier depth of its output
388:sentence – would have to separate two bare sets of `2 * k + 2` and `2 * k + 3`
389:elements, which `DescriptiveComplexity.StepDef.ifpHolds_equivK₂` forbids. -/
390:theorem even_not_ifpDefinableFree : ¬IFPDefinableFree EVEN := by
391:  rintro ⟨d, hd⟩
392:  obtain ⟨k₀, hk₀⟩ := d.exists_varBound
393:  set k := max k₀ (qdepth d.out) with hkdef
394:  have hbound : d.VarBound k := hk₀.mono (le_max_left _ _)
395:  have hout : qdepth d.out ≤ k := le_max_right _ _
396:  let : Language.empty.Structure (Fin (2 * k + 2)) := Language.emptyStructure
397:  let : Language.empty.Structure (Fin (2 * k + 3)) := Language.emptyStructure
398:  have : Nonempty (Fin (2 * k + 2)) := ⟨⟨0, by omega⟩⟩

FILE ROADMAP.md 1-120
1:# Roadmap
2:
3:Catalog of work **not yet done**, and of nothing else: an item is deleted when
4:it is built, never annotated as finished, the record of what the library
5:contains being `git log` together with the module docstrings. Organized by
6:theme; each item carries a rough scale of effort ([S] short, [M] medium, [L]
7:long, [R] research-level, i.e., the Lean proof would itself be a contribution)
8:and its prerequisites.
9:Main source: Immerman, *Descriptive Complexity* (DC below); also Garey–Johnson
10:and Karp's 21 problems for the catalog.
11:
12:## 1. NP-complete problems (catalog growth)
13:
14:Beyond Karp's 21:
15:
16:- **X3C** [M–L]: exact cover by 3-sets, from 3-Dimensional Matching or from
17:  Exact Cover; local gadgets, probably ordered.
18:- **3-Partition** [L]: strongly NP-complete, so the unary representation
19:  suffices and the hardness claim is honest; the classical source for
20:  packing/scheduling reductions. Warning: the 3DM → 3-Partition reduction is
21:  arithmetic-heavy; check FO-expressibility carefully before committing.
22:- **Bin Packing** [M after 3-Partition]: the standard downstream of
23:  3-Partition.
24:
25:## 2. Complete problems for other classes
26:
27:**Discharge symmetry** (guiding principle): each class-defining fragment (§3)
28:has a canonical complete problem that is essentially its *syntactic image*, so
29:each hardness discharge is a Tseitin-style translation of the defining logic
30:into the problem's vocabulary, i.e., a variation on
31:`sat_hard_of_sigmaSODefinable` with a shape invariant carried through. The
32:pattern is instantiated for every fragment the library defines: ∃SO → SAT,
33:SO-alternation-level-`k` → QBF_k, SO-Horn → HORN-SAT, SO-Krom → 2SAT (the last
34:two sharing their scaffolding in `ClauseDischarge.lean`), SO(TC) →
35:SUCCINCT-REACH and ∃SO[new] → FINSAT, so no discharge is outstanding; what
36:remains below are ordinary catalog reductions, drawings out of a machine, and
37:machine bridges.
38:
39:- **Monotone CVP** [M]: the unit-propagation circuit is monotone as drawn, so
40:  this is a matter of restricting the vocabulary rather than of a new gadget.
41:- **PSPACE, downstream of QSAT** [L, gadget-heavy]: the game problems
42:  (Generalized Geography…), the only PSPACE entries still missing.
43:- **Succinct problems, drawn out of the wide machine** [L each]: the classical
44:  second complete problems of the exponential classes are the succinct forms of
45:  polynomial ones, and the route to them is the machine, not the logic. A
46:  problem carrying its own locality is *drawn* by a reduction from a wide
47:  machine's run – which is how both tilings were reached
48:  (`Problems/Wide/TilingHard.lean`, `Problems/Wide/CorridorHard.lean`) – whereas
49:  proving it hard from the class's logic directly is a second construction of
50:  the same size. The generic succinctness theorem is **not** available as a
51:  route (§3), so each succinct problem is its own drawing.
52:  - **Succinct GAME** [L]: `GAME` is complete for PTIME already
53:    (`game_PTIME_complete`), and its succinct form is the classical
54:    EXPTIME-complete game problem. Bibliography to fetch from DBLP when the item
55:    is built – nothing from memory, nothing from a search snippet:
56:    `veith1997formulas` (Veith, *Languages represented by Boolean formulas*,
57:    IPL 1997), `gottlob1999succinctness` (Gottlob, Leone, Veith, *Succinctness
58:    as a source of complexity in logical formalisms*, APAL 97, 1999) and
59:    `balcazar1992succinct` (Balcázar, Lozano, Torán, *The complexity of
60:    algorithmic problems on succinct instances*, 1992, a survey).
61:- **EPR's hardness** [XL, low confidence]: `∃*∀*` satisfiability is
62:  NEXPTIME-hard ([Lewis 1980][lewis1980complexity]). The problem, its
63:  small-model property and its membership are built (`Problems/Epr/`); what is
64:  left is Lewis's simulation, and it is the real cost. Three things settle its
65:  shape, each paid for by the membership. **Reduce from a machine, not from a
66:  tiling**: a universally quantified matrix cannot say “*some* cell carries an
67:  accepting tile”, an existential over exponentially many cells, while a
68:  machine's acceptance pads the run to the clock and reads the *last* row, whose
69:  coordinates are a fixed bit-vector, so the condition is a guarded clause.
70:  **Coordinates are bit-vectors indexed by the instance**, one universal
71:  variable per element per coordinate, so an emitted symbol has arity `2n+1` –
72:  unbounded arity is what the encoding is for, and `sig` already carries it.
73:  **The increment of a coordinate needs auxiliary relations**, defined by
74:  clauses along the order of the instance: a carry chain is a disjunction of
75:  conjunctions and no single clause is that, whereas “agree above `k`” and “all
76:  ones below `k`” are forced upward by implications of fixed width, and upward
77:  is the direction the reduction needs.
78:- **Ruled out for these classes, and why** – do not re-propose: Datalog combined
79:  complexity (EXPTIME) is too domain-specific for a catalog meant to read as
80:  general complexity theory; regular-expression inequivalence with squaring
81:  (EXPSPACE, Meyer–Stockmeyer) needs an automata-and-regex layer that does not
82:  exist; Petri net coverability (Rackoff) and the commutative semigroup word
83:  problem (Mayr–Meyer) are counter machines, and unbounded counters fail the
84:  “numbers must be bitwise definable” rule; generalized chess, checkers and Go
85:  (EXPTIME) are tiling-scale simulations with a board layer on top.
86:- Δₖᵖ and oracle classes are blocked on machine models, presumably forever out
87:  of scope (§7 refines both judgments).
88:
89:## 3. Logics and framework extensions
90:
91:- **FO(LFP) ⊆ NP, directly** [M]: by guessing the fixed point and the derivation
92:  order and checking both first-order against the certificate interface
93:  (`derives_eq_of_closed_of_wf`). No new mathematics – the inclusion already
94:  follows by composing the FO(LFP) → SO-Horn translation with the Horn discharge
95:  – but the direct `Σ₁` definition would be textbook-faithful; the work is
96:  formula building, made tedious by the varying arities of a block's atoms.
97:- **Housekeeping in the shared machinery** [S]:
98:  `Problems/FinSat/Nodes.lean` imports `Sat/Tseitin.lean` for `NodeAt`, so if that
99:  cross-problem dependency ever grates, the node machinery is generic and
100:  belongs at top level. Beside it: `blockSym` / `repAssign` /
101:  `altAssign_qbfBlocks` in `Problems/Qbf/Membership.lean` are the monadic
102:  special case of `SecondOrderReplicate.lean` and should be folded into it –
103:  noticed while building the PH bridge, left alone because it touches a working
104:  file and bought that bridge nothing.
105:- **Composing an expansion with an interpretation, the outer way** [settled –
106:  do not reopen]: `DescriptiveComplexity.ExpExpansion.pullOrdered` composes an
107:  interpretation *before* an expansion (`A ↦ X.Map (I.Map A)`) and is what makes
108:  `ComplexityClass.exp` a class. The **other** order – an interpretation applied
109:  to an expanded structure, `A ↦ J.MapRel (X.Map A)` – is what a complete
110:  problem for an exponential class would need, and it is *not* an expansion:
111:  an expansion's defining sentences are first-order over the base with the block
112:  copies as parameters, while a quantifier of `J` ranges over the *points* of
113:  `X.Map A`, i.e., over block assignments, which is a second-order quantifier
114:  over the base. So the composite's relations are `Σₖ` over the base, not FO,
115:  and neither the plain composition nor a Tseitin description of the composite
116:  exists.
117:  **Quantifiers are the only obstruction**: an atom `R(x̄)` of `J` translates to
118:  `X.relSentence`, `x = y` to equality of tagged assignments, and `x ≤ y` to a
119:  definable order on the expanded universe, all first-order over the base;
120:  Boolean combinations compose. So the fix is quantifier-freeness, and it is the

313:  Gödel numbering of the syntax as finite structures, a definable satisfaction

323:## 5. Inexpressibility toolkit (unconditional results)
324:
325:The unique payoff of the descriptive approach: *unconditional* separations and
326:non-reducibility, impossible in the machine world.
327:
328:- **Further applications of the games** [M]: REACH/connectivity is not
329:  FO-definable, and non-existence of FO reductions in specific cases. The
330:  games are also the natural route to separating `≤ᶠᵒ` from `≤ᶠᵒ[≤]` below.
331:- **Locality (Hanf, Gaifman)** [L]: the workhorse for graph inexpressibility;
332:  gives connectivity/acyclicity results without bespoke games.
333:- **0-1 laws (Glebskii et al., Fagin)** [L]: FO 0-1 law on random structures;
334:  Mathlib's probability is ample. Fun, self-contained, good student project.
335:- **Order-necessity results** [R]: candidate research question the framework
336:  makes precise: show some catalog reduction (e.g., SAT → 3COL) provably has no
337:  order-free FO counterpart, separating `≤ᶠᵒ` from `≤ᶠᵒ[≤]` on concrete
338:  problems.
339:- Horizon: **PARITY not in AC⁰** ([Ajtai 1983][ajtai1983sigma11];
340:  [Furst, Saxe & Sipser 1984][furst1984parity];
341:  [Håstad 1986][hastad1986almost]) [R]: a switching-lemma formalization is a
342:  major standalone project. Everything around it is now in place – PARITY is in
343:  the catalog and in LOGSPACE (`parity_mem_LOGSPACE`), AC⁰ is a logic and sits
344:  inside PTIME – so this single theorem is what `AC⁰ ⊊ LOGSPACE` waits on. Do
345:  not confuse it with EVEN, the parity of the *universe*, which **is** AC⁰
346:  (`even_ac0Definable`) and is what separates `FO(≤)` from AC⁰.
347:- **`FO(≤, +) ⊊ FO(≤, +, ×)`** [L]: classically true, and *not* out of reach in
348:  the way PARITY is – primality of the universe is definable in the latter and
349:  not in the former, by Ginsburg and Spanier's semilinearity of `FO(+)` spectra
350:  ([Schweikardt 2005][schweikardt2005arithmetic] §3.2, which also collects the
351:  sources for `FO(<) ⊊ FO(+)`). That is a quantifier-elimination argument rather
352:  than a switching lemma, but Presburger quantifier elimination is not in the
353:  library either; re-price only against a concrete plan for it.
354:- Not a defect, an open question worth flagging as one: **expect no complete
355:  problem for AC⁰**. The library's reductions are `FO(≤)`, strictly *weaker*
356:  than AC⁰ reductions – that strictness is
357:  `exists_ac0Definable_not_foDefinable` – so an AC⁰-complete problem under
358:  `≤ᶠᵒ[≤]` would need a reduction that builds the arithmetic, which the
359:  separation suggests `FO(≤)` cannot do. Suggests, not proves.
360:
361:## 6. Beyond decision problems: counting and optimization
362:
363:Everything above measures *decision* problems. The non-decision world repeats
364:the same pattern, a syntactic class matching a computational one, with a number
365:or a relation in place of the yes/no answer: Saluja–Subrahmanyam–Thakur (1995)
366:prove `#FO = #P` with the hierarchy `#Σ₀ ⊊ #Σ₁ ⊊ #Π₁ ⊊ #Σ₂ ⊊ #Π₂ = #FO`;
367:Arenas–Muñoz–Riveros (LICS 2017; LMCS 16(1), 2020) give a cleaner framework,
368:**QSO** (Quantitative Second-Order logic), a restriction of Droste–Gastin
369:weighted logics to the semiring ℕ; on the optimization side there is
370:Papadimitriou–Yannakakis's **MAX SNP** (1991), and for numeric output
